subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL

speechtext: Mr. F. E. JAENICKE (Kindersley) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 154, to amend the Supreme Court Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the 13th January, 1947, the judicial committee of the privy council decided that the dominion parliament may, in the exercise of the wide amplitude of power conferred by section 101 of the British North America Act, vest the Supreme Court of Canada with final and exclusive civil and appellate jurisdiction within and for Canada and may accordingly deny any appeal to his majesty in council either from the supreme court or from any provincial court and regardless of whether the matter in question is within the exclusive legislative authority of the dominion or of the provincial legislatures.
The purpose of the present bill is to give effect to this decision of the privy council, and also to a previous decision respecting appeals in criminal matters, namely, British Coal Corporation v. the King in 1935.
Section 54 of the Supreme Court Act, which it is proposed to repeal by this bill, reads as follows:
54. The judgment of the court shall, in all cases, be final and conclusive, and no appeal shall be brought from any judgment or order of the court to any court of appeal established by the parliament of Great Britain and Ireland, by which appeals or petitions to His Majesty in council may be ordered to be heard, saving any right which His Majesty may be graciously pleased to exercise by virtue of his royal prerogative.
The right of appeal to His Majesty in council has been regulated in certain statutes of the parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, of which two are important:	the Judicial Committee Act,
83166-151J
Questions

1833, and the Judicial Committee Act, 1844. Both these acts are proposed to be repealed by this bill. The act of 1833 recites that:
. . . from the decisions of various courts of judicature in the East Indies and an the plantations, colonies and other dominions of His Majesty abroad, an appeal lies to His Majesty in council.
And proceeds to regulate the manner of such appeal. The act of 1844 recites that:
. . . the judicial committee, acting under the authority of said acts (the act of 1833 and an amending act) hath been found to answer well the purposes for which it was so established by parliament, but it is found necessary to improve its proceedings in some respects for the better dispatch of business and expedient also to extend its jurisdiction and powers.
The first section of the act of 1844 enacts that it shall be competent to Her Majesty by general or special order in council to:
. . . provide for the admission of any appeal or appeals to her majesty in council from any judgments, sentences, decrees or orders of any court of justice within any British colony or possession abroad.
This bill is in accordance with the decisions of the privy council here referred to, which themselves were based on the provisions of the Statute of Westminster, 1931.

The question before the committee is whether the five orders in council which have to do with Japanese in Canada should be continued for the life of Bill 104, roughly another year. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Moose Jaw suggests that P.C. 946 be deleted. P.C. 946 is the order in council which empowers the minister to exercise certain control over the movement of Japanese in Canada. It is obvious that if that order in council were deleted from Bill 104, no such power would continue, any settlement still being operated by the government would cease, any money being paid for the subsistence of Japanese in Canada would cease to be paid, and there would be nothing to prevent Japanese from moving about Canada at will.
The Minister of Labour referred in passing to the fact that an administrative order had been passed recently' which modified order in council 946. That administrative order No. 5, new series, begins by describing the coastal area, I take it that the description which follows is the description of what was hitherto known as the restricted area.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: As the protected area.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The boundaries are the same?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It sets out for the purposes of this order the boundaries of the restricted area. The order then goes on to say:
(a)	enter or reside in the coastal area; or
No person of the Japanese race shall
(b)	enter the province of British Columbia; or
(c)	travel a distance of more than fifty miles within the province of British Columbia; or
(d)	if resident in any place in the province of British Columbia, take up residence elsewhere in the province of British Columbia;
unless such person has obtained a permit in writing to do so from a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
So that any restriction on the movement of Japanese which had hitherto been applied under order in council 946 ceases east of the rockies. It seems to me that it would have been a simple matter to deal with these five orders in council on their merits, realizing that they are merely for the purpose of carrying on certain powers for a limited period. However, hon. members have seen fit to open up the whole Japanese question and to debate the whole issue, and that being so I feel it is necessary' to restate once more in as few words as possible the position which I take on behalf of those whom I represent.
Those whom I represent inhabit that portion of British Columbia lying immediately east of the restricted area. Long before the war a certain number of Japanese, perhaps between five and seven hundred, had resided there for a considerable time. It is not easy to say exactly what the number is today.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am speaking of the area which I represent.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, I am sorry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The best check I have been able to make is to -watch the issuance of ration cards in the last few years. The last figure I have for the district of which Kelowna is the centre is 665. At the beginning of the session I put on the order paper certain questions in connection with the number of Japanese residents, and in reply I received certain figures which have since been modified somewhat. As of January 31 there were 84 Japanese in the restricted area of British Columbia, I am given to understand that these were made up of infirm and sick persons in institutions and Japanese who had married white people and who were permitted to continue to reside in the coastal area. In the New Denver departmental project, one of the Japanese settlements in the southern interior, there were 949 persons. Those are the figures given to me and which appeared

Emergency Powers
in Hansard at the beginning of February. Elsewhere in the interior of British Columbia there were 5,727 Japanese.
I suggest that that is altogether too high a number of Japanese to expect British Columbia willingly to accept if the solution of the Japanese question is to depend upon their distribution throughout the nine provinces. As I pointed out, in the one portion of the Okanagan valley from which I come a total of 665 ration cards were issued to Japanese. In the mining city of Greenwood, whose population has sunk to about one-tenth of what it was forty years ago, a settlement was arranged and paid for by this government, but I have not been able to get the exact number of Japanese located here. Besides that, there is a total of between 5.000 and 6,000 in what might virtually be described as one-quarter of the province of British Columbia. It is obvious therefore that that province is being asked to assume a larger part of the total than is reasonable. The province with the largest number of Japanese at the present time is Ontario, and that figure is in the neighbourhood of 7,000. between
7,000	and 8,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Just under 7,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Then one-quarter of
British Columbia, in the southeastern portion, is asked to accommodate, to retain, pretty nearly as many as the whole province of Ontario, and that surely is not reasonable. I consider that those whom I represent, suffering as they have from this Japanese intrusion, have taken an extremely reasonable and restrained view of the matter. It should be remembered that even before the restricted area was set up by the British Columbia security commission, Japanese were beginning to trek out of what would be described as the restricted area, and in the Okanagan valley as well as in the valleys neighbouring thereto the Japanese population began to increase in considerable numbers.
It is true that the British Columbia security commission accepted the view of the inhabitants of those towns that as these people had moved out of the restricted area it was reasonable that they should be dealt with by the commission and put into the restricted areas which they set up, the camps or settlements or whatever they were, and to a large extent they were so removed.
To place the matter in more or less official wording, as from those whom I represent, I wish to quote a resolution which was adopted by the Okanagan and main line associated
boards of trade meeting in Revelstoke in January. The text of that resolution was:
That this association point out to the dominion authorities the danger of an influx of Japanese into the interior of British Columbia, following the expiry of the Emergency Powers Act on March 31, and urge legislation to prevent such a situation developing.
At that time the executive of the Kelowna board of trade wrote a letter similar to that which was addressed by the other boards of trade to the Prime Minister. I want to read a couple of sentences from that letter:
We have been advised that after March 31, 1947, all restrictions on the movement of Japanese in Canada will be removed and we are writing at this time to ask what action is being taken to implement the promises and assurances given by various government department heads that the Japanese would never again be allowed to congregate in one area. We strongly recommend that some government action should be taken to ensure that these people are evenly distributed, on a per capita basis, across Canada or some plan that will prevent them from again congregating in small areas in British Columbia. The people of this part of the Okanagan consider that there are already too many Japanese in this area and are most emphatic that no more be permitted under any circumstances. It is felt by this board that the government has had sufficient time to have formulated some plan, and I would respectfully request that we be informed of this at once. If nothing has been done, I would request that we also be informed of this.
To that, the replies from Ottawa appear to have been non-committal. The British Columbia cabinet ministers, including Premier Hart, replied sympathetically. Attorney General Gordon Wismer had written a strong supporting letter. That places the situation, so far as those whom I represent are concerned, in as succinct a light as I can put it.
The basis of their objection to the further intrusion of Japanese into that area is that they do not consider that the Japanese are assimilable. There are two courses which may follow the return of the Japanese to those areas. One is that they may nest themselves in cells, and that, I believe, the majority of Canadians who think realize is not a desirable way to deal with the future unity of this country. The other one is that there will be assimilation, that there will be intermarriage, that there will be children born of a type different from either of the two races who go to make up the marriage. Surely, looking at the world all over for two centuries past, there have been a sufficient number of dreadful examples of what has resulted from the creation of an Eurasian cast.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am enough
of a realist on this particular question to recognize that this is a vexatious prob-
Emergency Powers

lem in British Columbia, but the implications concern all of us in Canada, and for that reason we have a responsibility to help British Columbia to solve the problem. It is not enough for us merely to discuss it; we have to do something about it. It is our duty to see that each of the provinces carries out its responsibility.
I appreciate that the great concentration of Japanese in British Columbia was unfortunate. The Japanese were not entirely responsible for that. They were brought there to a great extent. In any event, the concentration led to discrimination, to persecution in some instances-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Where?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: -both on racial grounds and sometimes on security or on economic grounds.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In fairness to British Columbia the hon. member should cite those instances of persecution; for certainly there has never been any charge of persecution in our dealings with the Japanese.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have no instances of persecution at hand with me.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Why say it, then?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Instances have been brought to my attention from time to time, but I have not got them here at the moment. Looking at the picture generally, I do not think there can be any denial of it, but if the hon. member says it did not happen, perhaps he is in a better position to know.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You just don't know the picture; that is the trouble.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
With respect to the government's position on dispersal, it has been charged, and I admit that it was harsh and in many instances the Japanese have said that it was cruel. But it is argued that it was necessary in the public interest. As a matter of fact I think dispersal has had a beneficial effect, because it has introduced the Japanese to the rest of Canada. For a long time they thought that British Columbia alone was Canada, and it has introduced Canada to the Japanese. They have been accepted; in many instances they have been welcomed. They have set up new homes; they have started their lives anew. Yesterday the hon. member for New Westminster quoted the New Canadian as saying that the Japs are advising their people that dispersal is in their own interest, and if my voice is of any use at all, I too think it is in their own interest. I agree with those who advise that course of action, but I am not at all convinced, as are other hon. members of this committee, that 
if this restriction is lifted the Japs will immediately flock back to British Columbia. There are just as many fish in the Atlantic, I am told, as there are in the Pacific.
Let me refer to an article which appeared yesterday in the Toronto Star, written by Edward Yoshioka, a young man who studied at Emmanuel college in Toronto and had to return to Vancouver to be ordained. In part he says:
It does not seem right that Canadians have to go through all that.
He has to have a permit in order to go to Vancouver. He says:
My parents even had to get permits just to travel from Kelowna to Vancouver to attend my ordination.
The paper goes on to say that he is the winner of three prizes this year for theological studies. He was born twenty-four years ago in Vancouver, of Japanese parents. His father, Reverend Yoshinosuke Yoshioka, is a United Church minister at Kelowna. He came to Canada in 1919 on a scholarship won in Japan. He also studied in Emmanuel college. These are the significant words. Speaking of Ontario and the university of Toronto particularly, where he completed his studies, he said:
It has been wonderful here, and even during the war not one unkind incident occurred. Of course, conditions are more ideal here, but if only people would realize that though we may look different, wre are just as good Canadians as they are, then life would be happier for everyone. These regulations and restrictions really don't work severe hardship, but it's the principle of the thing.
That is my theme too. I could go along with the government during the war by backing the action that they took because they felt it was in the national interest and a matter of national security. They made a good case on that point; but in time of peace I see no justification for this order in council. On the grounds of principle I protest, because this puts an abnormal restraint on a Canadian citizen. It is tinged with racial discrimination and must outrage the conscience of all Canadians. What is more, this is a precedent, a precedent which will plague us for many years to come. So far as government policy is concerned today it is the Japs; tomorrow, well, who knows. Therefore we must be on guard and be awake to the dangers inherent in this order in council.
It is well to call the attention of the committee that racial discrimination is a phobia. It is just as essential to control as is atomic energy, because it too can destroy but from within. I am impressed by the speeches that were paade here by the various members from

Emergency Powers
British Columbia. No one sitting here and knowing the men who spoke could be less than impressed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How much impressed were you by the member for Skeena?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am afraid I took in too much territory. In any event let us forget the racial part of it. I am prepared to forget the economic part of it. One distinguished member of the committee put it on the basis of security. He said: "We shall make sure this does not happen in British Columbia once again." The committee was impressed by that argument. Let me prick the conscience of the committee. A hundred and thirty-one Japs served in the Canadian army. A hundred and thirty of them were Canadian born; one was a naturalized Jap. Some of them were wounded, and I believe some of them were decorated. We deny them the right to go back to British Columbia, to go back to a particular zone, though they may have come from that zone. That is going a very long way, and I point out to the committee how serious a matter this is. Certainly we are ahead of the United States with respect to that particular confinement. The most obnoxious racial laws which were ever passed in any country in the world, which were passed in nazi Germany, exempted for a time soldiers who fought on the battle front. Yet in endorsing this order in council we go farther than they ever went. I do not compare my government with them; I do not intend to make that comparison with any other government in this country, but on this Japanese question in all the democratic countries in the world we are now the foremost in racial discrimination. There is no rhyme or reason in refusing to these men, who served and fought for this country, the right to go where they like in Canada, though there may be administrative reasons for doing otherwise with respect to other people. I am whole heartedly and everlastingly opposed to discrimination on the basis of race or creed, or to any other discrimination, I feel that there is enough unofficial discrimination without my giving approval to what appears to me to be official discrimination.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I shall not detain the committee long, but I cannot let the previous speaker's words pass without an answer. Originally it was my intention to get the views of a cross-section of the committee but when words such as "persecution, harsh and cruel" are used, and when this country is described as the foremost in the world when
it comes to racial discrimination, I cannot let these words go unchallenged. It is all very well for an hon. member to rise in his place and make statements of that kind, but they should be backed up. In cold print I wonder what it would look like in Germany or in Russia. I know something about racial discrimination, because I visited these countries. I wonder how it would look in Great Britain or in South Africa. That is not the language to use in describing a movement of this kind, for the carrying out of which I have been charged with the responsibility. Let me say to my hon. friend that I do not take second place to him or to anybody in the country when it comes to treating my fellowmen in a humane way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: So long as they are not Japanese.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will my hon. friend wait just a minute? I come from a country which is pre-eminent in that regard, which has given shelter to people of all races and creeds.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: As no other country ever did.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, as no other country ever did. Let me say this to the hon. member for Spadina. Like myself, he was not born in Canada. The only nations in the history of the world that eveT fought for a principle were the nations comprising the British commonwealth of nations.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And they sacrificed everything for it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Of course they did. And when they accuse this government, or this nation at the head of which this government stands, of persecution, of being cruel, of being foremost in the policy of racial discrimination, the charge is not true, Mr. Chairman; and nobody knows that better than the hon. member for Spadina. This whole policy has been conducted in a manner which stands out preeminently, when one considers the movement which is necessary under war conditions of certain people of certain racial origins. I saw part of the liquidation of the Kulaks in Russia not far from where my hon. friend was born. I was in Germany when Hitler put over his revolution. I was in that part of the world when the Turks sent the Greeks from Asia Minor into Greece. I have been in most of those countries, and I think I know something about what persecution is and what cruelty is. Our policy was investigated by a representative of the Japanese government. I think it was done by the Swiss or
Emergency Powers

the Spanish, but it does not make much difference which it was. The point is that the policy was investigated and no complaint was found. I should like to know of any other government in the world which, when these people went back to Japan on a voluntary basis, would have paid their fares and given each grown-up $200 and each child $50. I should like to know of any other country which would have moved these people and taken care of them as they were taken, care of under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour. Let me say this to my hon. friend, with all the sincerity of which I am capable. I believe that our policy is in the best interests of the Japanese people themselves. My hon. friends over here who have been critical-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What about over there?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: All right; my hon. friend over here too, but he was at the war and is in a somewhat different position from that of some of my hon. friends.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is all right.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think every veteran in this house should stand up and repudiate that statement. There is no question of our loyalty. We had members in the forces. We served.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Just wait a minute. I want to say to my hon. friends that they have not got a first mortgage on the defence of liberty and freedom.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They think they have, and are trying to foreclose it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is the trouble with them. They think they have a first mortgage. We have sat here for a day and a half and listened to some harsh criticism, and we have taken it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You have not replied to the hon. member for Spadina.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The trouble with my hon. friends is they are so self-religious that they think they are the only people who are right; and when it comes to the expression of an opinion different from their own, they just cannot take it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You should reply to the hon. member for Spadina.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Let me say this. Before the interruptions took place-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Make way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not need to try to be funny, because he is funny enough anyway. Let me say that I would have felt in much better humour, if I can put it on that level, if the hon. member for Cariboo, who is an old friend of mine, and some of the other hon. gentlemen-with all the trials and tribulations which have been the lot of the Department of Labour in the past five or six years-could have stood up in their places and said they had formed committees in their communities east of British Columbia to receive these people of Japanese race and get them settled there. I should have felt in a much better frame of mind if they could have done that.
The hon. member for Victoria probably made the best speech, and the shortest one, on this problem. It reflected the basic principle of Christianity in everyday life. I think this-a.nd I think it sincerely, Mr. Chairman- that our policy has been in the best interests of the Japanese. The hon. member for Spadina vindicated that today when he said he had read-I think it was in the Toronto Star- about a minister of the gospel of the Japanese race who spoke in glowing terms of conditions in Ontario. I do not have to live in British Columbia-I sometimes think, thank goodness.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You cannot beat Ontario.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But I do know something of the history of the intermingling of the orientals with the white people in that province. I say that not in a critical sense; but it has been a problem for a good many years. I believe in the early days the present Prime' Minister went out under the direction of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and investigated it for the government of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: With Sir William Muloek.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, with Sir William Muloek. I am speaking now from memory. But there is no question about it, the information I get from my officials is that the people of Japanese race who have come east are much happier than they were in British Columbia. Is it not the sensible thing to do, to continue that policy-because in time, when we have them spread across this dominion, they will play their part in all its institutions and activities. I think it is much better than what I myself saw in British Columbia prior to the outbreak of the war, where there was a highly concentrated section of the community in the city of Vancouver which if I remember rightly they used to call Little Tokyo. What I should like to be able to do is to continue this policy

Emergency Powers
of dispersal-not by direction but by persuasion-which has been so successful up to the present time.
Notwithstanding the opinion of any man in this house or anyone outside of it without responsibility, if I had it to do over again in the light of the conditions which existed in 1942 I would do exactly the same thing, use exactly the same policies and treat our Japanese friends in the same humane way as that in which they have been treated under the jurisdiction of my department.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, despite the fact that there have been moments of heat, I think that those who have sat back and listened to this debate will recognize that it has been one of the best we have had on this subject for a good many years. Even though we have taken opposing stands and have got into some warm arguments, it seems to me that there has been a tendency to recognize sincerity and earnestness on both sides, which indeed befits a debate of this kind. Complimentary remarks have been made of some of those in this group who have stood firm on this matter through the years. I recognize likewise the sincerity and the earnestness of some of those who have taken a position with which I thoroughly disagree. I go even further and say that I take at their word those who support this order against Japanese citizens and who tell us that they are not doing so on the basis of any race hatred. I confess that in some cases as I listen to their speeches and read in Hansard the remarks that have been made it is a little difficult to believe that, but I take these members at their word. In particular when a member like the hon. member for Vancouver South stands up and speaks in the gentlemanly manner in which he did it is pretty hard to imagine that in his heart there is any hatred towards anyone.
I think too it is to be noted that there have been many efforts by those who have participated in this debate to make constructive suggestions. There has also been noted on the part of those on the other side a tendency to refer, as the minister did just now, to the Japanese as our friends. The hon. member for Vancouver South the other night made a plea for arrangements to provide restitution where the property of Japanese Canadians had been despoiled. All that is to the good. It suggests that in this parliament we have a reflection of the heart of the Canadian people, which is disturbed about this matter and which recognizes, as the hon. member for Spadina suggested, that the problem is a vexatious one but also, as he suggested, that
there is a principle at stake and that we are determined to move toward the achievement of that principle with all that it means.
I think it is significant that those who have spoken in favour of the continuance of this order, P.C. 946, have all felt that they had to make a case for the position they were taking. A few years ago that was not necessary. All one had to do then was to throw out a few inflammatory slogans and the case was taken as established, because in those days there was much more bitterness about the subject than there is now. Today members make their case on various grounds. Sometimes it is on defence, sometimes on race but allegedly without race hatred, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard suggested last night. He was quite forthright in saying that from his viewpoint the problem goes beyond the Japanese and includes the Chinese and East Indians. I respect him for the honesty with which he made that statement, but as I say, when I look at it in print and realize its implications I must state my disagreement with him.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Surely the hon. member realizes that the question he asked me was what the problem was, not my views on it. Is not that his recollection?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes. If that correction needs to be made to make everything perfectly clear, I am glad to make it. He said last night that he was endeavouring to give us what he believed to be the problem as British Columbia saw it, and he stated it in those terms. But you will notice, Mr. Chairman, that when he did so he was not throwing out slogans or telling us hair-raising stories, as was characteristic of previous debates on this subject, but was trying to make a reasoned basis for the position that he takes.
I want it to be perfectly clear that I disagree wholly with the members who are supporting this order, but I also want it to be clear that it seems to me that hon. members have made progress in their attitude toward this matter, and it provides a good basis from which to move on in the hope that even yet we shall achieve the full measure of the principle of which the hon. member for Spadina spoke a moment ago.
I do not blame the Minister of Labour for reminding us, as he did immediately following the remarks of the previous speaker, of the way in which the light of freedom burns in the United Kingdom, and that compared with other countries Canada has done a pretty fair job. I would be fully satisfied if we had in Canada the freedom so firmly established in the United Kingdom, but what we are con-
Emergency Powers

cerned about, and this is what makes the difference in a democracy, is not how well we have done in comparison with other places, especially lands where conditions may be a lot worse, but how well our achievements match our ideals and our principles and the things that we espouse. As the hon. member for Spadina said, we have been in a bit of a dilemma here in this house in discussing this matter. I have felt in listening to the radio reports about this debate that the vexatiousness of the problem has been made clear and also the compulsion of the ideals that are in the minds and hearts of most of us who are here.
Having said all that, I wish we could realize that what we are voting for in this order in council is not the sincerity or earnestness that may be in the hearts of hon. members; it is not the hatred or lack of race hatred that may motivate our speeches or our votes. This is a specific order which does specific things, and the fact is that this order in council does deny to certain Canadian citizens rights which other Canadian citizens are permitted to enjoy. I feel that all of us have to look at this thing very closely and in that light. The members from British Columbia have the right to ask those who do not live in that province to try to look at this thing from their viewpoint, and I think we all were impressed by the appeal which the hon. member for Victoria made last night. I may say to the Minister of Labour that I had the privilege of being on a committee of the Winnipeg city council in 1942 which arranged to bring some Japanese Canadians from British Columbia to that city, and I imagine that others of us in this house have done that sort of thing. I have also had the privilege in a personal way of extending my welcome to some Japanese Canadians now living in my riding, and I can say with the member for Spadina that I know that some of them are quite happy to be there. But after we have done all that, after those of us east of the rockies have met the request that the people of British Columbia make to us and tried to look at things from their point of view, I think that they also should realize that what is at stake here is a principle affecting the whole of Canada and our interest in that principle is a matter of supreme importance. You cannot divide Canada into different sections and have one principle obtain in one part and another somewhere else. We 5n this group applauded with eagerness the exchange of telegrams which the Secretary of State for External Affairs read today expressing the appreciation of the government of India for the action of

the British Columbia legislature in doing away with one bit of discrimination which has obtained out there all too long.
Speaking on this whole question of the principle of citizenship and of its being extended without any qualification to all people, I should like to make a brief reference to a recent book which has already been quoted in this house, the author of which has received a well deserved award. I refer to Arthur Lower's "Colony to Nation". In that book Professor Lower makes the statement that Canada is a supreme act of faith, and he goes on to underline that statement by pointing to the fact that normally one would not expect a nation such as ours to gain the position of strength it occupies, because of the difficulties we have had in welding various races together. But we have done so, he says, as a supreme act of faith.
He goes on to say that without tolerance, magnanimity, generosity and devotion to high principles, Canada just does not exist. I am deeply concerned that when we come face to face with a basic principle like this, always admitting that there are difficulties-and certainly there are in carrying out any high principle-we realize how fundamental it is to the very existence of this nation.
There are many principles without which Canada just does not exist. One of them, which is basic, is that there shall be no discrimination as between our citizens on the basis of race. There came to my desk today, as I imagine there did to the desks of all hon. members, a letter from the civil liberties association in Manitoba. The hon. member for Lake Centre, Mr. B. K. Sandwell of Toronto and I had the privilege not long ago of addressing a large meeting in the city of Winnipeg, held under the auspices of this association, when we discussed the whole question of civil liberties. I believe all will agree that this association has done a good job in the presentation of its six-point programme, each point of which is extremely important at this stage of our national life.
The first point, which is the only one I shall read at this time, because I am afraid the others would be out of order in this debate-although they are equally important -reads, under the heading "Declaration of Rights":
No Canadian citizen shall be exiled, nor deprived of his citizenship in any part, nor be discriminated against in the exercise of bis citizenship because of race, religion, colour, sex, language or political beliefs.
I know the Minister of Labour is likely to say it is easy to make speeches about these

Emergency Powers
high-sounding principles, but that actually one has to face up to the difficulties. That is right. And so are we right; and so is the hon. member for Spadina right, and so is my friend Arthur Lower right in suggesting that, without loyalty to principles like this, Canada just does not go on.
It seems to me it is extremely important, when a principle of this kind is being discussed, that we have a discussion of this kind in which hon. members express, in an honest and straightforward manner, the views they hold, as has been done in this instance. However I think it is also important, if at all possible, that the major political groups in the country give some definite and responsible expression as to where they stand on an issue of this kind.
Last night the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said he was reporting to the house what he felt to be the views of his constituents. I am not quarreling with the statement he made as being a report on the situation as he sees it, but I should like hon. members to read for themselves a paragraph from page 3 of a letter from the Vancouver consultative council, under date of March 25, 1947, which was addressed to all of us. I will read only a sentence or two to indicate the tone of the letter:
We are indignant that an impression has been spread that the citizen body of British Columbia is with substantial unanimity favourable to the perpetuation of such discriminatory measures. His Grace Archbishop Duke of this city selected a Catholic clergyman to act on the executive committee of this council and to serve as a member of a delegation which waited upon the Premier of British Columbia to protest against racial discrimination.
And then he goes on to refer to similar support given by private members and the responsible courts of other leading church bodies and leading persons in various political parties. The paragraph closes by saying:
The mere fact that hundreds of citizens of British Columbia, without regard to their various religious and political affiliations, have together made financially possible the work of this consultative council is itself evidence that the section of British Columbians sharing the views reflected in this letter is far from negligible.
I accept the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard to the effect that he believes that the views he expresses are those of the majority of his constituents. But they are not the views of all the people of British Columbia. As this letter, over the signature, by the way, of Doctor Norman F. Black, would suggest, there is a considerable body of people in British Columbia who feel as we do.

Mr. Chairman, the government made it quite clear through the Minister of Justice that this legislation rests squarely on a national emergency-that if the government is seeking to enact legislation which for the time being sets aside the constitution and gives it power to invade a jurisdiction which normally is exclusively that of the provinces; if it seeks to legislate by order in council where normally only parliament can; if it seeks to suspend the rights and privileges of the individual and the rights of citizenship, it is because a national emergency exists.
I voted against the second reading of the bill because in my opinion no national emergency exists. I brought forward all the normal
criteria by which the existence of an emergency is detected in peace, order and good government as well as in the realms of finance, industry, employment and trade. I canvassed the whole field, and no one attempted to contradict me when I showed that times are good, that employment is plentiful, that production is greater than it has ever been before; that foreign trade, both in imports and exports, is greater than it has ever been. Finding no vestige of evidence of the existence of a national emergency, I was forced to vote against this bill. I shall now say a few words about the orders in council which affect the Japanese.
The people of British Columbia are aroused over this question. They did not wish orientals to land on their shores. As I recall, it was in 1907 that the late Mr. Lemieux, once a much respected speaker of this house, went at the instance of Sir Wilfrid Laurier to Japan and there entered into some kind of understanding with the government of that country. It was called a gentleman's agreement, whereby the number of Japanese to come to Canada would be greatly restricted. Later, as some of us remember, there arrived off Vancouver a ship in which there was a large number of Indians, and although some of them bore on their breasts military decorations which showed that they had fought courageously and frequently in the defence of the British realm, they were not permitted to land. There were other instances in which the people of British Columbia expressed their wish that orientals should not come to their shores, but orientals did come. We are told that at the present time there remain in Canada about 23,000 Japanese, of whom about 17,000 are Canadian citizens.
The war was the occasion for the removal of the Japanese from the British Columbia shores of the Pacific. Some were moved to the interior of British Columbia, some to the eastern provinces. Now, two years after the cessation of hostilities-and I am dealing only with the Japanese who are British subjects- parliament is asked to continue the restriction and curtailment of the rights of these British subjects because of a national emergency.
In my view, Mr. Chairman, there is no national emergency. There is a keen desire, as manifested by many members from British Columbia-in fact, I think, by all members who represent constituencies which have returned followers either of the government or of the opposition-that these Japanese be not permitted to return to their former homes on the shores of the Pacific. Judging from the unanimity of Liberal and Conservative members, there must be a pronounced if not
Emergency Powers

unanimous feeling among the white population of the coast. I submit that that hostile sentiment is largely economic in its origin. It may be tinged by racial feeling but judging from what I have heard in the house, it is almost entirely economic; it is because the Japanese work harder and longer hours, live more cheaply and have made inroads upon the normal vocations and profits of the white population that they are not wanted in British Columbia.
That hostile sentiment may create a crisis but not an emergency. It probably does create a political crisis; but I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that the constitution of a country may not be suspended because of a political crisis. When there is a national emergency, when the life, the very existence of the country as a whole is in peril, then the constitution must yield to the doctrine of survival. But a political crisis is a mere incident in the every-day life of a country. A constitutional, representative government like ours comes in and is bound to go out, and it almost invariably goes out in a crisis, a political crisis. A political crisis is just as natural to our form of government as are three meals a day to a normal Canadian.
I submit that to contend that a national emergency has arisen because of this political crisis in one province is to make a travesty of our constitution and to endanger harmony among our people. Why does not the government deal with this crisis? Why does it not take this problem, which comes to it as a possible by-product of the war, if you will-

They came, and the war provided the people of British Columbia with an opportunity to get rid of them. They were moved away, and now the people of British Columbia are doing all in their power to prevent their return. The point I am trying to make is that that is not a national emergency. It is a political crisis, and I say to the government, why not deal with it as such?
If it is desired that there should be no more orientals in Canada; to be specific, if it is desired that there be no more Japanese in Canada, we are masters here in this Canadian land. Let us enact legislation to prevent other Japanese from coming here. I see no difficulty in that course. This is our home land; we alone may determine who shall enter here. I have heard it said, not by one but by half a dozen hon. members, that the Japanese have some loyalty other than a
[iMt. Hackett.]
loyalty to Canada. If that can be established -and it must not be established in the mass- if a Canadian citizen of Japanese origin has been a traitor to Canada, then the law provides a means for dealing with him.
Last year the hon. member who was formerly secretary of state put on the statute books the Canadian citizenship act, of which he was very proud. He conducted his bill through the house with great aptitude and persistence. By section 21 of this act Canadian citizenship can be revoked from anybody except a natural-born Canadian. How many of these
17,000	Japanese are natural-born Canadians I do not know, but let us divide the group in two. If any of these who have been naturalized have misconducted themselves, have been traitors to Canada, their Canadian citizenship can be withdrawn. The act provides the means, and they can be sent back to Japan. Their naturalization can be taken from them; they will cease to be Canadian citizens and will be sent back to the land of their origin. If there be Canadian-born citizens who are traitors, the law provides a summary way for dealing with them. But I submit that it is not wise, it is not well, to make wholesale charges of disloyalty against a national group. I am convinced that there are many Japanese, men and women, who are loyal Canadians, industrious and hard working, who are good citizens. If there be among the Japanese- and it is always well to remember that one of the twelve fell-one who has been unworthy of his citizenship, let him be detected, tried and dealt with in consequence.
I am reasonably certain that if the government were to say that no more Japanese were to be brought to Canada, much of the disturbance among the deputation from British Columbia would cease, and much of the unrest and worry which is being felt on the coast today would disappear. The difficulty is that the government is still waiting for something to happen. It is relying upon a fiction. It is creating an artificial emergency that it may Shield itself behind its shadow and like Micawber wait another year in the hope that something will turn up. If the government would accept its responsibility and meet the problems which confront it rather than try to put them off for another year under the assertion that a national emergency exists when none in fact does exist, we would be farther along our way to stability and order.
It is right and natural-and I am certain that if some hon. members from British Columbia speak after me they will do so-for hon. members to ask, what do you know about the Japanese? My answer is, nothing. They

Emergency Powers
may then say to me: It is very easy for you to be magnanimous and altruistic; it is very easy for you to be censorious of us; it is very easy for you to attempt the role of the statesman. We are under the harrow at home; our people are disturbed. They do not like this competition; they do not want the Japanese back. Under their breath they may say-they may tell me in intimacy, whether they are on this or the other side of the house: Our folk will vote against us unless we do as we are doing. I have been in parliament occasionally; I have been out of parliament a great deal. I do not know a great deal about the Japanese. I know a good deal about the irate electorate, and I have a great deal of sympathy for hon. gentlemen who are under its lash. But I want to make it clear that my experience with problems of this kind is not altogether negligible. I live, as do many hon. members of this committee, in the great metropolitan city of Montreal. Do not let British Columbia think it is the only province in the dominion which has had' perplexities arising out of the meeting of races. Do not let British Columbia think that it is the only province in Canada which has to meet the perplexities arising out of the meeting of races.
It has been said that we cannot assimilate the Japanese, that they congregate in groups and should be dispersed. I must say that I do not like these words. People come to this land not to be assimilated, not to be dispersed. They come because they believe it is a haven in which they can live their lives, worship their God and bring up their children in the best that is in their own tradition, and in the respect and love of the land which gives them the right to lead their own free lives.
I open a book. It is not a law book; it is not a treatise on government. It is a record called "The Census of Canada." I open it at a page which gives the population and the racial origin of the great metropolitan area of Canada. I turn to the city of Montreal, the home of thirty-odd national groups. I find that in 1941 it had a population of 1,139,921 people. Of that number 281,875 were of British extraction. There are 850,000 others. The French people represent the largest group, a little over sixty per cent of the total population of Montreal. The remainder come from the four points of the compass, from the seven seas and the five continents. They have come there and learned how to accommodate themselves to a common life. It has not always been easy. The French came first and they made it a little uncomfortable for the Indians.
Then the English came, and the Scotch came with them to see that the English did not get too rich. The Scotch were very mighty until the redistribution committee got after Muskoka-Ontario and levelled that fortress. Then there came from the mists of that green isle of the Atlantic, from that land of saints, scholars and fairies, the meek, the mild Irish. They did not inherit the earth this time, but they came to Canada about one hundred years ago, and some people did not like them. But they were woven into the Canadian web. Later, within my time almost, there came another element, an industrious element, thirsting for knowledge, a stiff-necked element, an element with an unquenchable spirit, one that has suffered in the last ten years as no race of men has ever suffered before, which indeed has been almost entirely exterminated on one or two continents. They came to the metropolitan centres and competed. They made it hard for the older races already there. They arrogated to themselves whole strata of business and drove out the English and the French. It was not easy to bear. Then after them came other central Europeans. This problem is not a new one. British Columbia has not made a great find. British Columbia is having just the kind of worry and embarrassment that the older centres have known and have endeavoured honestly to accommodate themselves to during the centuries.
Let me just say this in passing. It is the peoples who have learned to accommodate themselves to the presence of him who may not be his brother in colour and creed who have made of this land what it is. Oh, we have done great things. We have fought battles; we have developed a continent; we have manufactured; we have traded; we have won ourselves a status in many realms. But there is one thing of which we can be justly proud, and that is that we have found the way of making everyone who has come here feel that he had a dignity which everybody respected, and that once having acquired our citizenship he was inviolate in his rights. There have been no Jim Crow cars in Canada

I am not debating whether it was a mistake or not; but if it was a mistake, it was our mistake. We did it. Having issued that document, having made all those people Canadian citizens we should respect their rights. In Canada there is no dominant element. Canada, after all, is a country of minorities. The French are in a minority; the English are in a minority; the Irish are in a minority and the Scotch are in a minority. We are a people of minorities. The test of the government of a country is the way it treats its minorities. It is only if we can respect the dignity which is inherent in the human soul, if we can respect that divine thing which makes us brothers in God, that our country can be great and we can be worthy of the reputation which it has achieved. After that most terrible conflict in South Africa when the Britain and the Boer had fought each other and hated each other for years, when some measure was sought whereby harmony might be brought to these tortured peoples, where did they go? They came to the Dominion of Canada to find out how we had solved their problem. More than that, when, after 500 years of conflict, it was determined at last that there should be an understanding between Ireland and Britain, it was written into the preliminary document which preceded the treaty that the Irish should have what?-the kind of freedom which Canadians have.

We have achieved a great reputation in many fields, but the reputation which we have achieved in accommodating ourselves to the necessity of a common citizenship is the highest and most glorious of all. I do not wish to be understood as saying that I favour admitting to Canada this race or that race. I am for excluding any race that cannot fit into our national life. But there are some things that cannot be undone. If there are Japanese in this country today, it is not their fault. If they are Canadian citizens, it is because we placed the badge of Canadian citizenry upon them; and bearing that badge, it behooves us in honour to respect it. Possibly if I had had more courage I would not have made this speech; there are ho Japanese in my constituency. No pressure is on me. I have no one to reproach me but myself.

For the first time we are being asked to depart from those things which have made of us, I was going to say, a free people; for the first time we are asked to depart from the principles which the genius of two great races has evolved and which they have had 'the courage and the grace till now to apply.
I do not now say how I shall vote; I am waiting for somebody to deliver me from the necessity of separating myself from many whom I cherish and whose wisdom I admire and frequently rely upon. Unless I can be rescued from the position as I see it, I shall find myself forced to support the amendment, and I shall do so proudly.

I wish to speak briefly about what the order in council in its present form will do. I need not recapitulate the speeches which have been made about the attitude of British Columbia to the Japanese. I think it is a fair statement, however, to say that most of us did want the entire Japanese population of British Columbia sent back to Japan because we have found that, though they are a decent, hard-

Emergency Powers
working people, they do not become part of our life. But we cannot do that now because the supreme court of this country and the privy council have ruled that those Japanese remaining have the right to remain here, and so, faced with that, our task is to see that they are made into Canadians. In that task we failed before, and they failed even more than we did. They have hived together and sent their children to Japanese language schools or sent them back to Japan. It is true that there is not one British Columbia member who went to school in the province who did not sit in every classroom with Japanese students. But once they became adults, the gap started.
The only problem that I as a member of parliament am faced with today in regard to the Japanese is what is the best way to see that these Japanese do become real Canadians, Canadians not just by act of parliament but Canadians in thought and action and in loyalty to our way of living. All parts of this house are agreed that the old policy of the Japanese hiving together in Steveston and on the west coast of Vancouver island was bad, bad for us and bad for the Japanese too. Again and again in this house it has been said that the dispersal of the Japanese, spreading them all across Canada, is the only practical way of getting rid of the hostility towards them and of making them Canadians. The suggestion is that they should be allocated to the various provinces. That has been suggested very loosely by various speakers, but how are we to do it? Are we to take a roster of the Japanese and say that so many are going to Prince Edward Island, so many are going to New' Brunswick and so many are going to Nova Scotia. Obviously that is impossible. It would take an order more restrictive than the present order in council to accomplish that.
The hon. member for Spadina rather loosely used the word "cruel" in speaking of the movement of the Japanese. I think it would be a real cruelty to force the Japanese to live in certain parts of Canada, and I say that as a British Columbian.
The second suggestion was that it be done by persuasion. But any of us who know the Japanese well know they are just as fond of the coast of British Columbia as every one >f the nine members from that coast province is. Only last fall I spoke to a meeting of he Japanese in the coast town of Greenwood, where a large number of them had been relocated. A few of them came from my riding. They all want to go back to the coast of British Columbia and thejr were looking forward to March 31 when these orders in council expire, so that they could return.
Therefore, if we remove this order in council and leave it to the persuasion of people who are in public life and to the good sense of the Japanese we shall find in a year that the Japanese will all be back on the coast and back in those two industries in which they work so well, fishing and farming. If, however, the Japanese are given to understand, as they are by this order, that they are free to go anywhere in Canada and can pass freely back and forth except in this one narrow coastal strip for a period of years they will disperse- The Japanese in Winnipeg, it has been said, are very happy; the Japanese in Ontario are very happy. I know they miss the mountains and the sea just as we who are here miss the mountains and the sea. But they are surrounded by people who, I think, are treating them a little more kindly than they have been treated in recent years in British Columbia because of the old feeling there. I say that this order in council is the simplest and most effective way of seeing that the Japanese will disperse and will become the good Canadians that the Chinese have become in exactly the same way. We have never had the feeling against the Chinese in British Columbia that we have had against the Japanese, and for this reason, that the Chinese are spread right across the country. There are more Chinese in the city of Toronto. I am informed, than there are in the city of Vancouver, and when that situation applies to the Japanese they will be gladly accepted right across this country. So I have no tangle at all with my conscience in voting for the continuance of this order in council restricting the Japanese from that little coastal zone in British Columbia, because I believe that this is the only practical way in which these Japanese can be dispersed and can have the chance to become good Canadians.
In closing, I wish to say just one word in defence of the Minister of Labour. I listened with the greatest of interest to the speech of the hon. member for Spadina. He spoke well, but he used two words I think just a little loosely. He used the word "persecution." I defy him to bring forward in this house one instance of Japanese being persecuted in British Columbia. There has been hostility against the Japanese; there has been perhaps indifference, perhaps an unwillingness to accept the Japanese into our homes as we accept other people. But persecution, no.
Then the hon. member for Spadina reflected on the way in which the Japanese had been handled. He said that their movement was a cruel movement. Any movement of people away from the homes where they have
Emergency Powers

lived must involve heart-burning. When your people left the old land and my people left the highlands of Scotland there was heartburning at giving up the old associations and leaving the old home. There is bound to be that. But there is a great difference between that and cruelty.
Lastly, on this matter of high principle of which the C.C.F. have spoken so often, there is one member of that party who knows the Japanese really well, because he represents the north coast of British Columbia. He represents a great number of fishermen in the Queen Charlotte islands and elsewhere. But we have not found much principle in the way he has weaseled-to use the word of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni-against taking a stand as his colleagues have done. My point in voting against the amendment is that if it carried automatically we go back to the days before 1939 and we should find ourselves in British Columbia saddled with a problem which should be a national problem. Once again we would have the Japanese hiving in colonies in my riding, in Comox-Alberni and in New Westminster, and once again we would have hostility developing between that group and all other Canadian groups. And so, as the only practical way to ensure the dispersal of these Japanese across Canada, I am going to support this order in council.

speechtext:
The order in council under discussion involves a principle which, to my mind, is far-reaching, and for that reason cannot be treated lightly. I listened to most of the speeches in the debate, with the exception of a few made yesterday afternoon when I was unavoidably out of the house. I have taken the trouble to read some of them, particularly those of the hon. member for Cariboo and the hon. member for Kootenay East. I must say that, after listening to the debate in what I consider an impartial manner, I have not as yet been convinced to change the views I held originally in the matter.
The hon. member for Stanstead has expressed eloquently and ably the views I should like myself to express on this question. Today it is the Japanese; tomorrow it may be the Jews, and another year it may be another minority. I consider it is a dangerous precedent to carry on this order in council.
I must say I have a good deal of sympathy with hon. members from British Columbia who have expressed their views with great sincerity and their usual ability. As one hon. member from that province said, no one should cast any reflections upon them by imputing to them improper motives or accusing them of racial discrimination. I honestly believe they acted according to their conscience. They have expressed the views of their constituents, and that is what they were sent here for.
In this matter of racial discrimination I think it is fair to assume that nobody con-

Emergency Powers
siders himself guilty of such an attitude of mind. Hon. members who spoke in favour of retaining P.C. 934 have done so through a sense of duty. For us from the other provinces outside British Columbia I feel it should not be difficult to make up our minds as to what is the right thing to do in the matter.
The majority of those men who have been restricted in their freedom are Canadian citizens. The others are residents of this country, legally admitted to Canada; and as such they should enjoy the protection and freedom of other residents, as long as they abide by our laws. The reasons advanced by those who would have the Japanese kept away from the British Columbia coast have not impressed me. In the first place, there is the economic reason. Frankly I am somewhat dumbfounded that such an argument should have been invoked. It boils down to this, that in order to solve a simple economic problem we must deprive Canadians of elementary human freedom and fundamental rights. This, in my humble opinion, is unfortunate and an admission of incompetence. For that reason I do not think I should endeavour to answer the economic argument.
Then there is the security problem. Here again I fail to see what we should have to fear. There will always be traitors within our ranks, and they may not always be Japanese. There were none of them involved in the espionage inquiry, and I feel that the most subversive elements of our people are not Canadians of Japanese origin. So why single them out among possible disloj-al citizens?
So far as the alleged disloyalty of these people is concerned, I would rather take the word of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) than that of other hon. members who have thrown aspersions against them. Doubtless there is some truth in what has been said. But, after all, what does it amount to? What proportion of Japanese have been disloyal? Some of them fought on our side, and that should help to vindicate them.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) has said-and in this he was supported only a short time ago by the hon. member for Stanstead-the problem of the Japanese would be more easily solved if we knew exactly what our immigration policy is to be, and particularly as regards orientals.
Bear in mind that I do not find fault with the manner in which our immigration policy
has been carried out to this date. I think we are going about it in the right way. To my mind, the doors of this country are as wide open as we can afford to open them at this time. One thing is certain, and it is this, that we do not have to open the doors to oriental immigration just now. If at some future time we should have to do so, we could impose a number of restrictions which would not aggravate the situation in British Columbia. But let us deal with each problem as it comes before us. We are now facing the problem of Canadians who are restricted in their freedom. Those restrictions were very likely justifiable in time of war, for the same reason that it was then justifiable to send prominent citizens of this country into concentration camps, because of their political views. I think we are all agreed on this point. I understand that those who have been sent to concentration camps have now been released.
What about restrictions against Japanese? Is the present legislation to be continued, to be made permanent? If not, when is it to be abandoned. We have a duty toward those Canadians, but as yet we have no duty toward possible future immigrants of oriental races. So let us restore to our fellow Canadians their full rights as citizens; and when we deal with immigration of orientals in due course, we shall do it in the light of the solution we give to the present problem.
Speaking as a member of a minority group in the house, I make a special appeal to other hon. members who may represent minority groups, or who may belong to them. I want to appeal particularly to hon. members who come from Quebec and urge them to search their consciences carefully and to think twice before voting on this important matter.
I submit that it would be a dangerous precedent to maintain P.C. 946 one day longer than it is necessary to do so. Some hon. members have referred to the charter of the united nations. I am not particularly interested in that charter, but inasmuch as it embodies some of the principles of the great charter of Christianity which does not need to be defended in any deliberative assembly, I wish the charter of the united nations all the success it can possibly achieve.

(viii) make orders, rules or regulations respecting persons of the Japanese race as defined in these regulations, or of other persons resident anywhere in Canada who are wholly of the Japanese race, or who have a father or a mother who is or was wholly of the Japanese race, to prohibit such persons of the Japanese race or such other persons from moving or travelling anywhere in Canada, or from residing in any place or area in Canada, except subject to a permit issued by or on behalf of the minister and on such terms and conditions as may be prescribed by him or by any person .authorized to act on his behalf under these regulations.
As the hon. member for Restigouehe-Madawaska pointed out, when we pass a statute of this kind which selects one minority group on racial grounds, a group which has not been charged with having committed any crime, and states that their liberties are to be interfered with, we are taking a backward step. At this stage I should like to ask the ministry this question:	In view of the
opposition that has come from all sections of the house, will they be prepared to ask for a free vote on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Moose Jaw?

Perhaps the hon. member's judgment is better than mine and perhaps the judgment of the hon. members who have spoken is better than mine, but I ask them to consider the confusion that would result if 23,000 Japanese moved back into Vancouver. Let us be practical about the matter. I think we have been reasonably successful in the reallocation of these Japanese and have done it to the distinct advantage of them as individuals and of the nation.
I ask my hon. friend to take his mind back to 1942 when this matter was first placed under my direction. I think it was the hon.

member for Vancouver South who read a wire addressed to the Prime Minister of this country by a number of people in all walks of life in British Columbia. I know Grant MacNeil; I know7 Mr. Shewler and I know Mr. Winch, but I do not know the other people. I remember quite vividly the discussion that took place within the government and outside the government. They were fearful of the possibility of bloodshed unless this movement was undertaken. Frankly I believe it was the sound thing to do. I should like to think, when it is completed, there will be a reasonable reallocation of these people right across the dominion, but I shudder to think of what may happen if this amendment is carried. Assuming it is carried tonight; tomorrow morning these people could start back to the coast and no doubt many of them would.
In Ontario there are, at the moment, close to 7,000 Japanese. I have never noticed them around because they constitute only a pebble on the beach in a population of 3,500,000. They have more or less moved into the life of this province. In Quebec there are well over 1,200 and they have moved into the life of that province. The same applies to Manitoba and the- other provinces. We have to be careful and not get away from the principle involved. I have the figures in front of me but I do not want to clutter up the minds of hon. members with them. You do not need figures when you are dealing with a principle.
I have known the hon. member for Vancouver East for a good many years and I know he has never changed his opinion. When he expresses an opinion, it is a matter of conviction. I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Stanstead. Let us not lose sight of the practical feature of this matter. There is a possibility of something almost like a trek back to Vancouver and one or two other centres in British Columbia. Many of us in eastern Canada have never seen a Japanese and it is all very well for us to get up and talk about them when we are not confronted with this problem.

I am charged with the responsibility for this matter, which is an entirely different matter from just making speeches. As I say, there will probably be a trek back to Vancouver and other centres in British Columbia where the Japanese were highly concentrated. I agree in the main with the hon. member for Stanstead, but you have to look at the other side of the medal. I think it is far better to attempt to establish the Japanese across this country than to be faced with the condition that might arise in some of the centres of British Columbia if this amendment were allowed to pass. That is the practical thing to consider.
I wish to say this to my hon. friend who has just spoken and to the hon. member for Stanstead. I take second place to no one when it comes to defending the freedom of the individual, and so far as we are concerned we are prepared to take the vote at any time. I cannot speak for the government but I cannot have any objection to any member arguing the question from the point of view of principle. I must point out, however, that, as the minister administering the department, I am faced with a practical situation and I would rather face up to it courageously. There is an emergency, whether you like it or not. You may argue, if you will, that there is no emergency, but I would ask my hon. friends this question. Suppose you had a tremendous influx into the city of Vancouver, in short order, if this amendment carried, would they consider that an emergency? Would you not call upon the government of the country, or upon the province or the municipality to face up to the problem?
In a broad and general way we have used every measure of common sense in approaching this problem in the interests not only of the people of British Columbia but of the Japanese themselves. I have studied the discussions that have taken place in this house ever since it was decided that their movement from the Pacific coast was necessary, and I hope we shall use the same good sense on this occasion as w'e have shown in the past, so that in the passage of time a point may be reached where everyone will be more or less satisfied.

There are several questions I should like to ask the minister, and then there is a statement which I think it is fitting should come from this group. I will not ask the minister to answer the questions as I put them. He can do so afterwards.
It would be well for the committee to have these questions answered, however, before this general debate is concluded. Can the minister tell us the number of Japanese from whom property was taken as a result of the exigencies of war? What measures did the government employ to ensure that each unit of the property was appraised at its full financial value? What precautions has the government taken to see that the Japanese owners shall not be permitted to suffer financial loss? Has the minister prepared a detailed report on all financial relations between the Japanese and the government?
My reason for asking these questions is that, in my opinion, the members of the house should have a report as a result of the perusal of which they can determine for themselves whether or not we have been in any way unfair to the Japanese in a financial way.
In my judgment, no Japanese must be allowed to sustain any financial loss as a result of any exigency of the war for which that Japanese was in no respect personally responsible. I believe that is a sound principle upon which the members of the house ought to act and to act sternly and justly. It would indeed be a reflection on this country if it were to be proved that Japanese had suffered financial loss.
May I turn now to the matter of discrimination. Much has been said about racial discrimination. Social creditors are unalterably opposed to all forms of racial discrimination. But social crediters are aware-and let some hon. members bear this in mind, for it is a thing which they are overlooking-that certain forces are designing to discriminate against the white race.

umbia, whose fishing rights were infringed upon by the Japanese, were not being discriminated against, right under the eyes of this government? How is it that we have heard no voice raised in this house in defence of the Indians against such discrimination?
