My position is clearly established. Will anyone seriously argue that the white people of British Columbia, who have seen the Japanese invading the British Columbia small-fruit industry, are not being discriminated against? Can it be successfully maintained that when Canadian governments in the past short-sightedly admitted Japanese to British Columbia soil, against the protests and pleading of the people of British Columbia, they did not discriminate against the white people of British Columbia?
We must be realistic in these matters. It is easy enough for the white race to stand up so straight that it falls over backwards, and that is what a good many members would seem to wish to do today, so that their children and their grandchildren will wake up some day and find their rights as Canadians destroyed, given away in a moment of foolish sentimentality. Can it be denied that the present government, if it permitted Japanese to return to British Columbia and multiply there, and extend their economic, social and political strength in that province, would not be guilty of rank discrimination against the white people of British Columbia?
Social crediters are opposed to discrimination against the white race in Canada as well as discrimination against every other race. Social crediters are opposed to discrimination against the people of British Columbia, and social crediters are opposed to discrimination against white Canadians yet unborn, generations and generations of them.

Now may I stop here to make a comment in support of the minister's remarks regarding those people who never saw a Japanese. Why, the men and women in this country who have never seen a Japanese, who have never lived near Japanese, have no right to pronounce upon the subject at all. Let them listen to the people who know about the Japanese, the people who have lived near them and have seen what happens, the people who understand. How is it that men fail to appreciate this truth? What sort of intelligence or logic would there be in my rising to pronounce upon problems peculiar to Prince Edward Island when I have never been there? I listen to Prince Edward Island people on those problems. Let Canadians listen to British Columbians on British Columbia's problems.

Social crediters therefore propose to stand by British Columbia members and the minister in their courageous effort to safeguard and guard the rights of the white race in British Columbia. Nobody is fond of speaking when he is not wanted to speak, but I wish to make a few brief comments. I find myself so much in agreement with the hon. member for Stan-stead-we always like to vote together-that I find it- difficult to vote against this amendment. But I intend to vote against it and I wish to say a word or two to explain why. I am sure he did not, but he spoke in a way that intimated he thought that people who had taken part in civil liberties associations were a lot of cranks. I should like to suggest to him that that is not so, although there was a tendency that I am very well aware of for all kinds of people to crowd into civil liberties associations and, in some cases, turn them from their original and valid purposes.

Emergency Powers
I wish to say two things about this resolution. It seems to me that, while it is not correct to say we have a war emergency at this time, at any rate we have a hang-over from a war emergency. It seems to me that we have not yet found a way to deal permanently with this situation. I am not going to take up the time to discuss whether it is the fault of the government or not. We should have been farther on the way, but we do not seem to be at the point where we can make a wise decision. To me there is great force in what is said by the people from British Columbia, that if this thing is decided in this way, if it is brought to an end now it means that the other provinces push back on them this whole problem. I do not think that is fair. I remember once the late Lord Tweedsmuir said the difficulty was not when you were faced with right as against wrong but when you were faced with one right against another right.
I find myself in genuine difficulty; nevertheless, for the reasons which I have given, while having full respect for the principles laid down by the hon. member for Stanstead which have to guide us in our eventual dealing with this matter, at the moment I do not think we are right in pushing it back on British Columbia. Therefore I shall vote against the amendment.

There is a specific case which I wish to bring to the attention of the committee to show the committee exactly where it has put itself by its vote on this amendment. This case may not be an isolated one. If the committee can find some way of justifying this treatment 'there may be some reason for having voted against the amendment. Yesterday I received a letter from Vancouver, written on behalf of a Japanese Canadian veteran of the last war who was evacuated from the west coast defence zone. The name of this man is Inouye. His regimental number is 228458-S. He was wounded and received an honourable discharge. Before evacuation he had a small farm near New Westminster, the legal description of which is given in the letter. For some reason or another, perhaps because he was a veteran, the farm was not sold. It is rented. The war being over for two years, this man is now seeking permission to return to his farm, but permission is refused. Permission cannot be refused on the score that he is disloyal. He has proved his loyalty by fighting for this country, as a matter of fact by offering 83166-152J
his life in defence of the country. He had worked on this farm. It is the work of a lifetime. He was deprived of his farm, not because he was disloyal but because it was deemed necessary in the interest of Canada that for a certain time persons of the race to which he belonged should be moved from the Pacific coast. As a matter of fact this man comes in the category of persons who were referred to in 1920 by Captain Mackenzie, who is now the Minister of Veterans Affairs, when he said in the legislature at Victoria that these British subjects have vindicated the fundamental essentials of citizenship and an acceptance of that principle lay in the extension of the franchise. If that was right-and I submit it was right-by what process of logic or reason or of justice can this man now be denied the right to return to his farm?

It demonstrates so clearly what this parliament, representing the principles of liberalism and the principles of freedom which the British people represent, denies to a man who fought for this country. Now I want to ask the committee this: what are you going to do with this man? Where stand all your professions of freedom, liberty and justice now?

speechtext: On the practical problem.

speechtext: Yes, in a practical problem. Can anyone suggest that the return of this man to his farm in the Fraser valley, in British Columbia, is a danger to the security of Canada? As I mentioned before, here you have a man who was willing to make the supreme sacrifice for the country of his adoption, and you tell him, "You must remain in a concentration camp while somebody else lives on your farm."

Just before the dinner recess I was saying a few words in regard to the case of a veteran of world war I which came to my attention. I thought I had just about finished, but the Secretary of State made an interjection which caused me to decide to say a little more. During the past two or three days I have listened to so much rationalization in this chamber that I really have had to keep fairly good control over myself in order not to get excited about it. I have listened to people who know their position is wrong trying to rationalize themselves out of it. You cannot rationalize yourself out of a wrong position. I have lived' long enough to realize that the only way one can do right today is to have done right yesterday, and the only way you can do right tomorrow is to do right today.
I shall try to give expression to the few words I have to say tonight without rancour, without racial prejudice or anything of that kind. As a matter of fact I feel quite sure I do not harbour any racial prejudice myself. I believe the Scottish race is the finest race on earth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I object, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have come to that conclusion because so often I have heard them say so, at Caledonian societies banquets and Burns suppers. The Secretary of State took exception to my saying that the veteran of world war I, to whom I referred before the recess, who cannot now get back to his farm at New Westminster, was in a concentration camp. Perhaps that was an extreme statement of the case, but the fact of the matter is that he cannot travel beyond a certain radius without a police permit, and a person who cannot do that is pretty close to being in a concentration camp. Certainly he is not a free Canadian; certainly he does not enjoy the freedoms for which he fought between 1914 and 1918. I am informed that Mr. Inouye, the man I referred' to, has written many times to the authorities in Ottawa, and cannot get anywhere. The party in Vancouver who wrote to me in regard to this case said he saw Mr. Mackinnon, the commissioner or placement officer, who told him there was nothing he could do about the matter; that at the present time there were some four or five war veterans in Vancouver but they were there under special permits, and they either had to leave when those permits expired or had to have the permits renewed.
I should like to know what would be the attitude of the war veterans in this house if

a white war veteran could not go to Nova Scotia, for example, without a permit. I am quite satisfied that every war veteran here would rise in his place and object to that sort of thing. If that is the case, as I am sure it is, the only reason there is not the same concern in this instance is that this man's skin is brown, and that he is of the oriental race. That is not good enough for the members of this house, nor, in my opinion, is it good enough for this government.
I am going to refer for a moment to the dispersal policy, and I hope the Minister of Labour will not take what I am about to say as personal criticism of himself. On more than one occasion I have made the statement in the house, and in letters to the minister I have said on several occasions, that I thought, under the circumstances within which he had to work, he did a good job. But I am going to say that in dealing with this matter the Minister of Labour was not a free agent. I am going to say that the cabinet itself did not give him the support he should have had to deal with this matter, that the cabinet allowed itself to be blackmailed into dealing with these people as it has done. That is why we are in our present position. Certain political promises were made that these people would never return to British Columbia. Then, once we got them out of the province, every attempt was made to make conditions so tough for them that not only would they not go back to British Columbia, but they would leave the country altogether. I am not blaming the Minister of Labour for that, but I am surprised that in the cabinet there were not men who loved freedom enough to insist that these people should have a fair deal.
As to the dispersal policy, is it any wonder it was found difficult to disperse these people, since we tried to disperse them and at the same time attached to them the stigma of disloyalty? They were sent out of British Columbia as enemy aliens. Is it any wonder that other provinces did not want to take enemy aliens? The first thing the government should have done in its dispersal programme was to make clear to the provinces and the Japanese themselves that they were not enemy aliens. As a matter of fact, as the Minister of Labour has indicated, they were removed, not only for the protection and security of the west coast, but also for their own protection. And they should have been treated, not as enemy aliens but as wards of the state. Their property and persons should have been scrupulously protected.

Emergency Powers
But that is not what has happened. Their property has been despoiled. The minister suggested today that they would rush back to the coast. Very few of them can go back to the coast, because there is nothing for them to go back to. And I am not at all in agreement with him that they would suffer any violence if they went back. The same thing was said with regard to the Japanese evacuated from the Pacific coast in the United States if they returned. But they went back, and there "was no violence; there were no disorders. A few people did try to make trouble. But the good sense of the people in the Pacific coast states of the United States recognized that these people were American citizens, and should receive the protection of the government of the United States. I am satisfied that Canadians are even more law-abiding than our American neighbours, and I am quite sure that nothing serious would happen if the Japanese should go back to British Columbia.
But I do not want them to go back. In so far as I have been able I have urged them to settle in other parts of Canada. I have numerous letters on file from those who did go to other parts of Canada, and who have told me that they are getting along well.
If the government wanted them to settle in the other provinces, would not the logical thing be that, as soon as they went into those provinces, all restrictions with the exception of returning to British Columbia should be removed? But what happened? They went into these provinces, but they could not buy property. They could not move from place to place. They could not make long distance telephone calls. People who are placed in that sort of position cannot acquire the social and economic roots which are necessary for permanent settlement. And it is only quite recently that those restrictions have been removed.
All this talk about dispersal is, in my opinion, too late. It is far more difficult today than it was during the last three or four years. In regard to irksome restrictions, I have in mind a particular case, which I mentioned in the house before. The government of Saskatchewan took into its employ a young Canadian Japanese lawyer who had graduated from Dalhousie university in 1942. Because of conditions prevailing at that time, although he was ready to be called to the bar, the bar association in Nova Scotia, decided it was not desirable that he should be admitted to the bar at that time. He returned to Ottawa and did his best to get into the armed services. He could not do that. Then he got work somewhere in Saskatchewan, and a year or so
ago was taken into a position of responsibility in the civil service of that province. Then he learned that, the war being over, he could now be admitted to the bar of Nova Scotia. But could he go to Nova Scotia as an ordinary Canadian citizen would? No; he had to have a permit from the mounted police to move from Saskatchewan to Nova Scotia to be admitted to the bar of that province.
Is it possible to get people to settle under conditions of that kind? It is folly and nonsense to think that can be done. So I say the first mistake that was made by the government when these people were removed was that they were designated as enemy aliens, and treated as such when there was no question whatever as to their loyalty.
I listened with pleasure and admiration to the great speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). There was one part of it particularly which appealed to me, and that was where he said that if a person were disloyal or subversive the thing to do was to bring him before the courts of the country and determine his guilt or innocence through those courts; but that the innocent should not be punished indiscriminately with the guilty.
We have been promised a. loyalty commission. On August 4, 1944, speaking in this house on the same question, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said this, as reported on page 5916 of Hansard:
What is clearly needed is the establishment of a quasi-judicial commission to examine the background, loyalties and attitudes of all persons of Japanese race in Canada to ascertain those who are not fit persons to be allowed to remain here. The commission I have referred to should, I think, be established in the fairly near future, in order that it may begin what will be a large and important task. The result of the work of the commission would be to establish a list of disloyal Japanese persons some of whom will be Japanese nationals, some British subjects by naturalization, and some British subjects by birth. The government's intention would be to have these disloyal persons deported to Japan as soon as that is physically possible.
That was on August 4, 1944. But no commission has yet been appointed to do the work proposed. Then in December, 1945, when the three famous, or infamous, orders in council were passed, one of them provided that a loyalty commission should be appointed. But the commission was not set up under that order in council. In December, 1946, it was again mentioned that a loyalty commission, or some sort of commission, should be appointed to look into the loyalty of these people. But no commission has yet been appointed for this purpose, although it
Emergency Powers

is nearly three years since the Prime Minister said that what was clearly indicated was the appointment of such a commission.
In my opinion there is only one reason why no such commission was appointed, namely, that there was no disloyalty to investigate. And because no such commission was appointed, after several promises were made, the government should now say to people of Japanese origin in Canada, Canadian citizens as most of them are, and to those who are not Canadian citizens that, no fault having been found with them, they should now be allowed to take up their place in this country as citizens and as residents. That is what is indicated by the actions and words of the government itself.
^ I was glad that the hon. member for Vancouver North, w'hen speaking this afternoon, made it quite plain that he was not basing his claim for the exclusion of the Japanese from British Columbia on the score of the security of the province. If I understood him aright he based his reasons for wanting to keep them out of the province squarely on economic grounds, on the ground that if they were permitted to return to the province they would interfere with the employment of white residents. All I can say to that is that if economic conditions in this country are such that a mere handful-there are only about three or four thousand men, women and children

of people coming into British Columbia will upset the equilibrium of the economic situation in that province, then this government must be making a bad job of rehabilitation. However I am convinced that his economic fears are as baseless and as groundless as are the security fears of the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
When an effort was made to disperse these people across the country, not only were they considered as enemy aliens but everything that could be said in their favour was suppressed and their opponents were allowed to carry on their vilification without restraint.
I have in my hand a report which appeared in the News-Herald of Vancouver under date of February 8, 1946. Under the heading, "Suppressed report says Japs save beet' sugar crop", the report states:
There can be little doubt that unless Japanese labour had been recruited, the great bulk of the crop would not have been seeded, with the consequent loss to Canada of many thousands of tons of beet sugar. The Japanese performed an important and essential function in maintaining sugar beet production in Manitoba and Alberta. In 1943 it was estimated the Japanese in Alberta alone provided at least $750,000 worth of necessary labour.
fMr. Maclnnis.]
The Japanese on the prairies have developed religious, cultural and recreational facilities in the areas where they settled. They have participated in community enterprises, church and youth organizations, sports teams, victory loan and Red Cross drives. While concentrating mainly on sugar beet work, the Japanese on the prairies also helped in general farm operations.
W'hy should a report like that be suppressed? Why not let the people of Canada know?

One of the two federal government reports dealing with the evacuation and resettlement of Japanese in B.C. and which were withheld from the public during the war, says-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

myself. Since I have not that opportunity and since it would not be fair for nm to exercise it if I had, I have to say these things when I get the chance. However I am going to leave the matter there. I am convinced as strongly as I have ever been convinced of anything that we are adopting the wrong-attitude in this matter and that we cannot build, not only a united world but a united Canada, on a basis of that kind.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think in an evolutionary way my hon. friend's mind travels very much like my own. I think I mentioned it this afternoon, but I want to say to my hon. friend that he has certainly shown a degree of sincerity which the hon. member for Skeena did not show yesterday.

speechtext: I have shown as much sincerity as the minister ever did.

speechtext:
There is one thing
about my hon. friend, he has been consistent down through the years, even from before the outbreak of the war when he raised a question about a returned soldier. My mind goes back to 1941 or 1942 before the Japanese were in the war, when the British government, for reasons best known to themselves, insisted that the wives of all British subjects in Hong Kong should go to Australia. There were a great many resolutions passed by wives of British residents that they wanted to stay with their husbands, which is a natural thing for any woman to do. I remember the criticism of the British government at that time because of the action they had taken in regard to that matter, but time has vindicated their action.
My hon. friend speaks of enemy aliens. I had something to do with prisoners of war in this country, since those who ^ worked in civilian pursuits came under my jurisdiction. At the outbreak of the war the British government, I would not like to say arrested, but took under their control many people of many races, and there were those in Great Britain, and possibly in Canada and in the United States as well, who contended that such persons should have been allowed their freedom. Well, that is the price you have to pay when war breaks out. The government is charged with the responsibility of the state, and you cannot conduct a war successfully from a soap-box or on the basis of sentiment. War is war, and you have to make decisions in the light of the conditions and circumstances as they exist at the time, irrespective of the complexion of the political party that happens to be in power.
I am still convinced that our policy was a correct one in connection with these people of Japanese origin. I recall flying to Vancouver when it was decided that this mov ement should be made. When I got off the train I met a certain group in that city and they spoke to me about a policy I was setting in motion. I said to them-I will not give the committee the whole story-"I dont know whether you know it or not, but you may be living in the twilight of a civilization, for I have had' some experience with the Japanese.
I served with them out in Singapore in the last war and they have merely the veneer of civilization. If they should come to the Aleutian islands or into British Columbia or further into western Canada they would, if necessary, wipe out every man, woman and child in that part of the dominion." There was a real threat at that time.
Hong Kong was lost in two weeks, Singapore in six weeks, and the Dutch East Indies in twenty-four hours. The Americans had lost every effective capital ship in the Pacific, the Australian army was in Syria, and the state of defence in Australia was of a character that would make even a courageous man quiver. That was the situation at that time.
My hon. friend speaks of enemy aliens, i do not think they were ever treated as enemy aliens.	.

The hon. member speaks of concentration camps. I do not like the words "concentration camps". The hon. member for Spadina used what I term European language in reference to a question of this kind. A concentration camp, as understood in Europe, is something entirely different from the sort of camps in which these people were housed in Canada. There is no comparison whatever. Do not let us use the jargon of the communist party when we are talking about Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I do not like to hear these words and phrases, which are jargon in Europe, used in reference to the Dominion of Canada. We have had no concentration camps as far as the Japanese m Canada are concerned', during the time they were under my jurisdiction.
I know what a concentration camp is. I have been to Europe and I have seen the countries where they existed. My hon. friend spoke of a young Jap who wanted to go to Nova Scotia, I believe. There is no law against that.

I say to my hon. friend that we have, in my judgment, the fairest system of judiciary of any countiy on earth, not excepting Great Britain; and when it comes to freedom of speech I do not make any exception either to that statement.
Aly hon. friend spoke of a loyalty commission. It is quite true that the statement he referred to was made by the Prime Minister, regarding the establishment of a loyalty commission. If the hon. gentleman's mind will go back, he will remember that, prior to the defeat of Japan by the allies, over 10,000 Japanese in this country wished to return to Japan voluntarily. After the defeat of Japan, that number was reduced considerably, but upwards of 4,000 went back voluntarily, which, in my judgment is, to speak the language of my hon. friend, a pretty fair vindication of the policy of the government, and an assessment of the loyalty of the Japanese individually.
Mr. AlacINNIS: I do not agree with you.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
You are not asked to agree with that statement. I am putting forward that point of view. These people wanted to return to Japan and we paid their fares and gave them $200, on landing, for each adult and $50 for each child.
May I say this. I said it before and hon. members will forgive me for the repetition. I would like to think that our soldiers in Hong Kong, that the Canadian civilians in Japan or the Americans or the British were treated as well _ as we treated these people in the Dominion of Canada.

Emergency Powers
Let us be frank and honest about the matter. I said that my hon. friend himself is moving very much in the same direction as I am. During the dinner recess I looked up this quotation from a speech he made on August 31, 1946. It will be found at page 5722 of Hansard and reads as follows:
These restrictions should be completely removed except as regards the return of persons to Pacific defence area.
These words were used less than a year ago. I say to my hon. friend that we are moving in an evolutionary way to meet this problem. Less than a year ago in this House of Commons my hon. friend said that the Japanese should not be permitted to return to the Pacific area. I agree with him absolutely that it is not in their best interests as a group; that they should be relocated across this dominion. I agree with him from that point of view. But it takes time to do these things. Since the policy was enunciated in 1942, the problem of the Japanese has not been such a difficult one so far as I and my administration are concerned, but I must say that it was intensified by some of the speeches which have been made in this house. I am frank to admit that some have to talk to the boys back home. I have no objection to that at all. I forgive them for it. I think I have covered all the points raised by my hon. friend, but I know he is thinking of this returned soldier.

Before we leave this
matter, I wish to ask the minister three questions. I am glad he forgives me for "talking to the boys back home". In regard to Mr. Inouye, will the minister investigate the case, and if he has any discretion in the matter will he see what he can do with it?
My second question is, has any official request been made by the government of Alberta for the removal of persons of Japanese origin who were moved to that province shortly after the evacuation? Has the position of these people in Alberta been clarified? Will they be removed from there, or may they stay there if they wish? If they have to be removed from there, what provision is being made for settling them elsewhere? This is an important issue, because they should not be removed when the beet growers have finished producing their beet crop and there is no work for them elsewhere. They should be removed, not at the best time for the beet growers, but at the best time for Japanese.
The third question has to do with the loyalty commission. I mentioned that there 83166-153
were three definite statements made in regard to the loyalty commission, one in August, 1944, one in December, 1945, and if my memory serves me rightly, another one in 1946. Surely either that commission should be appointed or a statement of the government made and publicized that there is no disloyalty to be investigated.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The first question has to do with the soldier. I shall be glad to look into that matter.
The second question is the Alberta matter. At the moment no request has been received from the Alberta government. As I indicated yesterday, the Japanese there can move out at their will so long as they do not go back to British Columbia. Of course there is a problem in Alberta. The sugar beet crop in Alberta and in Manitoba and, to a lesser degree, in Ontario was saved by the fact that we had Japanese labour in those three provinces in the last three or four years. That is a matter of fact, not a matter of argument.
The third question had to do with the loyalty commission. I would think that when the order in council was repealed-I am merely expressing a personal opinion now- and the power of deportation was ended, the loyalty commission became unnecessary because there has been no suggestion to my knowledge of deportation by compulsion. All the people who have gone to Japan have gone there voluntarily. I hope that answers my hon. friend.

speechtext: One other question about Alberta; has any request come from the beet growers of Alberta that these people should stay there for another year? I believe there was a conference on the matter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have met the beet growers from Alberta. I am speaking from memory now. I cannot be too sure about it, but I am under the impression that they have also made representations to the government of Alberta. It is obvious that you have to get the crop off. The Japanese people assisted materially in getting the sugar beet crop off in Alberta.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I
should like to ask the minister a question. I have two cases, one of which has already been referred to in the house, that of Sergeant Buck Suzuki. The leader of this party brought that case to the attention of the house last year. This man was bom in Canada. I am told that his parents have been in Canada for thirty years. He served with great distinction in the Malaya cam-

Emergency Powers

paign. While he was fighting with the British forces overseas, presumably for democracy, his wife and children were moved to Toronto and -his house and land, which were valued at $7,000, were sold for the sum of $1,963. I do not know whether Sergeant Suzuki received that amount or not.
The second case is that of Yasuzo Shoji. He was wounded twice with the Princess Pats in the first world rear. In British Columbia he had a two-story house, nineteen acres of land, four chicken houses, at least 2,500 hens and an electric incubator. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Of course, while the bill to amend the act may be introduced on Monday, it may not be debated for some considerable time. In any event I have a few remarks I should like to make tonight, having to do with these orders in council and the general question of old age pensions. The four orders we are now considering deal, in the first place, with an increase of $5 granted on August 10, 1943, under the War Measures Act; a further order in council passed on May 29, 1944, which restored the privilege, existing before the passing of the first order, of having an annual income totalling $125 over and above the pension; the other two orders in council refer to pensions in the Northwest Territories. I have nothing directly to say about them this evening, though my general remarks will apply to them as well as to old age pensions in other parts of the country.
In my opinion, there has been an utter failure on the part of the government to realize the plight of the old age pensioners of Canada, our other older citizens, and our blind. This failure has been most noticeable with regard to the amount of the pension, which is too low for a recipient to live decently in many centres of Canada. In addition, the regulations are too severe, so that in some cases applicants are completely disqualified from receiving the pension, and in other cases where pensions are granted the amount is reduced by reason of the stringency of the regulations.
When old age pensions were first introduced in Canada the lead was taken by the dominion government. That was back in the twenties. At that time it was not a question of waiting for the provinces to move. The dominion government took the lead. The same was true in the early thirties, when the government of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett increased the

Emergency Powers
proportion of the pension payable by the dominion from fifty per cent to seventy-five per cent.
But in recent years the dominion government has not been taking the lead in old age pensions matters. . It has been hiding behind the provinces. In support of that contention I would refer hon. members to the statement of policy made by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) on November 14, 1941; at that time he was Minister of Finance. He admitted in this statement that there had been requests from various parts of Canada for the dominion to pay a cost of living bonus to the old age pensioners. But he declined to grant that increase. Ail that he offered was that if any province saw fit to make a special supplementary payment, the dominion, very graciously, would not as a result reduce the dominion's contribution to the regular old age pensions payments.
At page 4428 of Hansard for November 14,
1941,	the minister is reported as follows; and here, I think, we have the basic policy of the government on old age pensions:
The dominion must, I am convinced, take the position that old age pensions of the non-contributory type now in effect are primarly a provincial responsibility, the role of the dominion being that of a contributor financially assisting the province to discharge this responsibility.
In other words, the government then took the stand, in November, 1941, that the primary responsibility for old age pensions was with the provinces, and that the lead must come from them.
In the following year, 1942, the situation of old age pensioners in Canada had become so desperate that some of the provinces began to pay supplementary grants. The first one to do so was my own province of British Columbia. They made provision in January,
1942,	for the payment of an additional amount of $5, bringing the maximum in our province up to a total of $25 a month for single pensioners.
The then minister of finance here in Ottawa was questioned about that situation in February, 1942, and in explanation of the British Columbia provision we find him stating this, as recorded at page 498 of Hansard for February 11:
The dominion government makes no contribution to the additional $5 a month. The position of this government was made clear in a statement which I made to this house in November.
Then a few days later, on February 17, the minister quoted from a speech by the premier of British Columbia, made at the time the supplementary grant was passed in that province. The premier used these significant words; and, mind you, this was five years ago:
The government of the province has given careful consideration to this matter and is of the opinion that conditions in British Columbia warrant the increase of old age pensions to $30 per month, and, pending appropriate action by the dominion to that effect, it proposes to supplement the pension now paid by $5 per month. Of this amount $2.50 is the provincial share of the increase recommended-
That is one quarter of the recommended total increase of $10, which would have brought the pension to $30 a month.
-and the other $2.50 represents a war-time cost of living bonus, which will cease if the scale of pensions is increased by the dominion before the cessation of hostilities.
Subsequently other provinces demanded an increase in the general rate of pension. For example, in May, 1942, Manitoba demanded an increase, and I have here the statement of the then minister of finance with regard to that request from Manitoba.
I have here also a statement by the minister on April 1, 1943, when, again, he was being pressed with respect to an increase in old age pensions. He was being urged to have the dominion take some steps toward increasing the pension, and we find him taking this stand as reported at page 1769 of Hansard:
Essentially the question is one of jurisdiction; and the position which this government has taken, and which I announced in November, 1941, is that we regard the responsibility for old age pensions as primarily one of provincial jurisdiction, just to the same extent as mothers' allowances, for example.
I have never been able to bring myself to the belief that old age pensions and mothers' allowances are in the same category. I think that the dominion then, in 1943, was still hiding behind the provinces.
Then, two or three months later, in July of that year-

I do not know about that. They may have done so. Perhaps if the dominion government had not been quite so extravagant it would have been possible to have both.
Then in 1945, nearly two years ago, we had the dominion calling a conference with the provinces. The dominion got out for that conference a nice green book, a copy of which I hold in my hand and which, by the way, I understand was given out to the press before being given to the premiers of the provinces. This book is entitled, "Proposals of the government of Canada." In those proposals hon. members will find the admission that old age pensions are much too low. That is to be found right here in the dominion's own proposals. Of course that was only confirming what was contained in the report by Doctor L. C. Marsh, published on March 16, 1943. Both those government documents suggested that the minimum should be at least $30 a month, and both suggested that the age should be dropped from seventy to sixty-five years.
The main objective of the dominion in making those proposals was to persuade or force the provinces to give up certain taxation powers which the dominion government had enjoyed during the war by virtue of agreements made with the different provinces. One subtle way of bringing pressure to bear on the provincial governments to give up those taxation powers was to hold out to the Canadian people the attractive social security programme to be found in this green book, including increased old age pensions. The dominion was hoping all the time that Canadians, when they saw those proposals, would demand that the provincial governments accept them and hand over the taxation powers. In fact the dominion was using the old age pensioners and the older people of Canada who would be reaching the age of qualification, as a pawn in the dominion's game with the provinces. Let me put it another way-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman is too much of a gentleman to really be serious in making that observation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The minister of National Health and Welfare need not put it on the basis of gentlemanly conduct.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is the way it should be.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not make statements in this house which I do not believe, and I believe the statement I have just made. For the benefit of the minister I will repeat it. In my opinion the dominion, in effect, was using the old age pensioners and the elderly people of Canada who would be reaching the age of qualification, as a pawn in the dominion's game with the provinces. Or let me put it another way: using them as a club to force the provinces to accept and to give up taxation powers.
In any event, be that as it may, it is clear now that there is no possibility of agreement at an early date and it does not help the elderly people or the blind of Canada one bit for the dominion . to try to place the blame on the provinces. The onus is right back on the dominion government to give a lead in settling the old age pensions problem. The onus is right where it was in 1926 and 1927 when the Old Age Pensions Act was first passed.
Finally, a word about the regulations. These regulations are much too severe. I do not need to rely only on my own opinion in making that statement. It is found right here in both government reports to which I refer, the report of August, 1945, and the Marsh report of 1943. These regulations should have been eased long ago. It does not require any big dominion-provincial conference to ease them. Demands have been made in this house at every session. I made them
Emergency Powers

myself in 1945 and again in 1946, that the regulations be changed, and the Minister of National Defence, who was then Minister of Health and Welfare, promised on December 15, 1945, that he would call together a meeting of the representatives from the different provinces to deal with the regulations. He had not done so at the time the session of 1946 ended, but finally there was a meeting in December, 1946. As yet, however, there has been no announcement by the government of any change in the regulations. The minister from British Columbia, under whose jurisdiction old age pensions come, returned from Ottawa on December 6 of last year and I have here an interview with him upon his return. He hinted that the pension rules might be eased. He said that the committee which had met was purely advisory as to the dominion's Old Age Pensions Act. All the provinces apparently are waiting for the dominion to announce what changes are to be made in these regulations.
I do not need to go over the details of the regulations to show their unfairness. That is shown by the very fact that only forty per cent of the people of Canada over seventy years of age have been able to qualify under the regulations. That figure is taken from the dominion's proposals of August 1945, at page 37. Doctor Marsh gave the percentage as from forty to forty-five. There are some glaringly hard regulations. One is the method of computing income. Take the regulation under which an applicant can be deemed to have a certain income because he has certain property, whereas in fact he may not be getting one cent out of it. That has always been a most unfair regulation.
Then there are the residence rules. I suggest that the regulations should be changed so that twenty years in Canada after the age of eighteen would be sufficient to qualify, with perhaps three years' residence immediately preceding application. Why should not changes be made such as we made last year in the War Veterans Allowance Act? After careful consideration by a special committee on war veterans affairs last year, a recommendation was brought in that the recipient of war veterans allowance could have his own home of a value up to $4,000 without having it taken into consideration in applying for war veterans allowance. There should be the same provision for old age pensioners. Under the War Veterans Allowance Act there is provision for casual earnings up to $125 a year. I do not see why there should not be the same regulation under the Old Age Pensions Act. The two acts were supposed to be similar. The War Veterans Allowance Act 
was improved last year, and there was no reason why the Old Age Pensions Act could not have been improved at the same time.
In closing, may I emphasize the importance of the time element. Time means so much when one gets up to that age. Every member of this house regards time as very important right now. Those of us who are only fifty or forty years of age begin to realize the importance of time. Put yourself in the position of the applicant for an old age pension, who is seventy or sixty-five years old. Time is of the utmost importance, and there should never have been this long delay in meeting the tragic position of elderly Canadians and of the blind people across the country. I repeat that that delay has been a disgrace to the nation and, in particular, a disgrace to this parliament.

Emergency Powers
other hon. members, including my genial and now smiling friend- the hon. member for Calgary West, risen often enough to demand action on this matter.
The orders before us have to do with continuing the basis as it now stands until the new legislation comes into effect. So far as I can see, no one will vote against these orders in council. One could not consider letting the present amount drop to the $20 provided in the act. But the point that some of us have been trying to make-and it seems to me it is important to make it now when the resolution is just about to appear on the order paper-is, in the main, the one that the hon. member for Vancouver South emphasized in his closing remarks, namely, that time is of the essence. It is not just a matter of the various ages which the hon. member for Vancouver South referred to; it is a matter of weeks and months in the lives of the old people who are now waiting for an improvement in their old age pensions. They certainly should not have to wait any longer; that is my plea to the government.
I rise particularly at this time to say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that, unless the resolution which is to appear on the order paper on Monday really goes some decent distance in improving the needs of our old age pensioners, he had better use the time between now and Monday to redraft it.
There are some discouraging rumours abroad in the country at this time. One of them is that the new legislation is to provide for an increase in the amount of the pension to $30 a month. All the strong words that the hon. member for Vancouver South used will have to be applied to that figure. It simply is not enough for our old people to live on.
Earlier this session the Prime Minister made a specific promise that when the new bill was brought in it would cover everything that we now have in the order in council which is before us plus something more. I suggest that $30 a month now is not something more than $25 was when the Prime Minister made that promise on February 4. On account of the increases in the cost of living, $30 a month now for old age pensioners is actually something less than they were receiving at the time the promise was made. Therefore I urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare to consider seriously the effect upon the morale of our old people, the effect upon the spirit of our Canadian citizenry generally before he brings in that resolution for such a meagre amount. What is needed for our old people is a
pension on which they can live in dignified retirement. We of this group say it should be not less than $50 a month. We say too that the time has come to lower the age; that the pension should be payable at an age not later than sixty-five. It is also extremely important, if this is to become a pension and not just a form of charity, that the means test with all its viciousness be removed. Further, if an old age pension is to mean what it should to our older Canadians there should go with it a cost of living supplement to fluctuate as the cost of living index moves up and down. There should also be with it a provision for hospitalization and medical care.
Almost every time there is a debate on the question of old age pensions, remarks, sometimes by way of an interjection, are passed around as to there being sympathy in all quarters of the house, sympathy on the part of all members for our old age pensioners. No one denies that for a moment. There is an abundance of it here. I am quite satisfied that at any time across the years had members had an opportunity to vote for improvements in our old age pensions legislation, had there been a free vote the majority would have been overwhelming, if not unanimous. But the point that really matters to our old people is not the sympathy that is expressed or any claims as to who has a monopoly on concern for the old people; what counts is definite action to improve their lot by providing a pension on which they can live.
I do not wish to go over the history of this matter again; it has been done quite thoroughly tonight by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I do not altogether concur in his contention that the dominion is hiding behind the provinces. Actually that is only one side of the picture. I think he has used the wrong figure of speech. Buck-passing is the proper phrase. The dominion has been saying that it is a provincial matter; but in the provinces, even those provinces that have made some increases, it is felt that the matter is one which is up to the dominion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does that apply to the Saskatchewan government?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The Saskatchewan government, like the British Columbia government, both of which have made increases, as well as others, have- done so out of practical sympathy for the old people in their provinces, but they feel that the final responsibility for a proper Old Age Pensions Act rests here in Ottawa.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
What are the total pensions in these two provinces?

Emergency Powers

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The total pension in British Columbia is now $35 a month; the total pension in Saskatchewan is S30 a month, plus hospital, medical, optical and dental care free to all old age pensioners as well as to certain other groups.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In British Columbia it is the same.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I believe they also get medical and dental care in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, there is something of that kind, but it is not as all-inclusive as in Saskatchewan. I am not concerned about pitting these provinces against each other. I say, as I have already said in answer to the hon. member for Lake Centre, that even the province of Saskatchewan, which is doing the best it can-and I am proud of it-for the old age pensioners, feels that the final responsibility for a proper Old Age Pensions Act rests with the dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Is it not a fact that Saskatchewan is now paying less than some other provinces?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The fact is that the hon. gentleman who advocates $50 a month supports the only government in the dominion where his political ideology is in power and which has not paid as much as some other provinces.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I deny that. When you add to the cash payment the value of the hospital and medical care on an over-all basis which is given to the old people of Saskatchewan, they are right up with all the rest of them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member a question.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member had better go out to the Saskatchewan legislature and ask the question there. He had the chance to do it but he did not take it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
