speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You will not do that next time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member for Rosthern if, as a citizen of Saskatchewan, he is not proud of the improvements in social legislation which have been made in his province in the last few years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I dislike seeing the old age pensioners having to pay more than $5 for hospitalization'-having their old age pension taken away from them in part when they go into the hospital.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
They do not. You do not know what you are talking about.
Mr. KNOWLES': That is not correct.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I ask if this is a private fight or a public fight? I really should like to listen to the hon. member. He is always interesting, even though he is usually wrong; but I want to know how far wrong he is.

Emergency Powers

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for Calgary West for reminding me to remind the committee that all remarks should be addressed to the chair and that hon. members should not interrupt another hon. member who is speaking, unless they have his consent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I want it to be clear that, in the province of Saskatchewan old age pensioners and others receive, through the medium of a card which entitles them to it, their hospital and medical care and benefits free. These things were given them even before the general hospitalization plan was enacted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Old age pensioners and others.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not often interrupt, Mr. Chairman, but may I ask if it is not true that the Saskatchewan citizens pay a per capita fee of $2 for that medical care?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Not the old age pensioners.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am glad to know of this interest in the situation in Saskatchewan. I should be quite willing to go on answering questions, but I think I might leave it. After all, there are a number of Saskatchewan C.C.F. members in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Let us get to the old age pensions bill as quickly as possible.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Absolutely. What I was starting to say before I had these interesting questions was that the old age pensioners have been the victims of this game of tossing the responsibility back and forth from one place to the other, and we feel that the time has come to settle that responsibility where it belongs, namely, with the federal government. I was going to mention that in the province of Manitoba the issue has come up. The hon. member for Vancouver South spoke of the demands that province made a few years ago for an increase in the pension, and it is true that at one time they added $1.25 before the federal government made its $5 increase of 1943. No further increase has been made in that province, and only recently-in fact, this very month-a resolution introduced in the Manitoba legislature calling for that province to make a $10 increase, just for the period of time until the federal government increased its pension, was turned down. The resolution was introduced by Mr. M. A. Gray, a C.C.F. member for Winnipeg. It was the combined vote of Liberals and Progressive Conservatives that defeated the motion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Why does the
C.C.F. not raise it to $50 in Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan asked the Saskatchewan government the same thing that he says someone asked the Manitoba government today?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Think of your own
responsibility in these matters.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I will.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I can carry this on just as well as anybody else, but all this is doing, Mr. Chairman-even my part in a free-for-all of this kind-is demonstrating the fact that the old age pensioners are the victims of the back and forth political talk that we have in this house, that we have between dominion and provincial governments, and that we have right across the country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The most political statement I have ever heard made here is the one you have just made.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am prepared to accept my hon. friend's remarks, provided that we can get down to the fact that the time has come for a government somewhere-and we contend that the responsibility rests with the government of the Dominion of Canadar-really to do something about this whole question of old age pensions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I go right along with you there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is fine. At last we have agreement. Now I want to say this, and I will sit down.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I really should not get applause for that, because I have said it several times before and it always gets applause.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Stay with it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The thing I am most concerned about now, in addition to the provisions of the act that the minister says will be on the order paper by Monday, is its effective date.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I said the resolution.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, the resolution. The hon. member for Vancouver South has referred to the importance of time. The promise to the old age pensioners of Canada that something specific would be done was made
Emergency Powers

in the speech from the throne on January 30, 1947. That promise was confirmed by the Prime Minister on February 4 when he said that the amendments forecast in the speech from the throne would include all we have now, plus something more. It may be all right for us in this house to let time slip by, but it is not fair to the old age pensioners. My hon. friends over there are laughing. They have had the opportunity, the right and the authority, from the day this session started, to put old age pension legislation on the order paper, but they put it off, for one excuse after another. When we first asked questions about it the Minister of Justice said that the matter was the subject of discussion with the provinces. Then a little later, when we began pressing for it, we were told that it was a matter of priority. Now we are being told that we must wait until we get this debate over; in other words, an attempt is being made to blame the house for the government's own delay in placing this matter on the order paper. The fact is that it could have been placed on the order paper any time after the day the speech from the throne was read. I say now that the proper thing for the government to do for the old people of Canada, when they do bring down this legislation, is to make retroactive to January 30 the payments that are to be provided under this act. Nothing less will be fair to the old people of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
This is really the first opportunity members of the house have had to discuss the old age pensions question, and be thoroughly in order and thoroughly fair to the other members of the house. I believe that should be borne in mind when we are appraising the amount of effort that some members have made with respect to the old age pensions question. We have been in session since early this year but have not had a chance, except on the speech from the throne, to discuss old age pensions. That is unfortunate. I feel, however, that it is only fair to give credit to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for the persistence he has shown in this matter.
I have no desire to occupy any great amount of the time of the committee, but I do wish once more to put our group on record with respect to old age pensions. Those who have been members of the house for some time will recall that, a good many years ago,
I began to advocate $50 a month for people sixty-five years of age and over. There should be no means test. I do not intend to burden the committee with any amount of elabora-

tion. I just wish to state the bare skeleton of the case, so that others may have the floor and speak also. There should, I repeat, be no means test. I consider that the means test today is a most irritating and unbecoming thing to be using in the Canadian system. To think that a man who is getting a meagre pension like $30 a month is denied the privilege of going out, even in his old age, and earning additional money without being in danger of losing his pension is a most discouraging, disheartening and altogether undesirable state of affairs. The means test should be abolished completely with respect to old age pensions. There should be no restriction whatever on the additional earnings of anyone who has gone beyond the age of sixty-five. Surely if a man or woman can go out and earn money in addition, after that age, he or she should be permitted to keep it.
Then I believe the pension must increase with the years. I know how unpalatable this will be to many hon. members who think in terms of orthodox finance, but we simply must face certain facts. The severe taxation structure in this country is rendering it harder and harder for anyone to save for his advanced years. It is at the same time rendering it harder and harder for young people to get enough money ahead to care for their parents. Consequently the pension simply must increase with the years.
Then the age at which people receive the pension must gradually decline. There is no use in making wisecracks about taxation and how it must be reduced. The simple, inescapable fact is, that the age at which people receive the old age pension must become lower and lower with the years, for the simple reason that it is becoming increasingly difficult for people over forty-five years of age to get jobs in this country as we begin to return to anything like normalcy. Let us face up to that situation and govern our thinking and planning in accordance with those facts.
In addition to the matters I have already-referred to, hospitalization, medical and dental care must be given free to elderly people. I do not think I need say anything more about, that; it is perfectly clear.
The question will be asked, where will the money come from? As the Minister of Justice indicated, it is obvious to every hon.. member that it is going to be impossible to raise by taxation the money which will be necessary to give the elderly people what they ought to have, to provide the other social services the country ought to have, and to accomplish the many other things everyone in the house knows we should accomplish. It must be obvious beyond any shadow of doubt

Emergency Powers
that there will have to be such a change in the financial system of this country as will render financially possible that which is physically possible.
Now may I say a word or two as to what is physically possible. May I once more remind hon. members that in 1944 this nation produced $11-8 billion worth of goods which, divided among twelve million people, amounts to about $983 for every man, woman and child in the nation. Let me recall what other hon. members have pointed out, that at the time we produced that $11-8 billion worth of goods we had some 700,000 of our finest producers overseas, and a very large percentage of our productive capacity engaged in war work, purely for destruction. Now those 700,000 and more are back from overseas. There is no longer any need for that productive capacity to be used in war production.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Gladly.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member mentioned that in 1944 we produced $11-8 billion worth of goods. What kind of goods were those, and how many of those goods are in demand by the Canadian people today?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is a very logical and fair question, and I accept it. But surely the same energy that went into the production of tanks will produce trucks, butter-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Wheat.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Let us go through it point by point; there is no contention between us. I should like to spend a minute or two on this, since hon. members are very much interested. Into that $11-8 billion worth of production went the beef we were producing, the wheat we were producing, various kinds of grains, pork, eggs and all that sort of thing. Surely we can produce just as much of those commodities now that we have those 700,000 young men back again as we could when they were overseas; there will be no doubt about that. The same factories which were producing guns can now produce nails, wire and the other things we require. The factories which were producing battledress and clothing of other kinds for our soldiers can now produce civilian clothing. One could go right on down through the list and show that we* could just as easily produce $11-8 billion, or probably $12 or $13 billion worth of goods and services in this country on a peace-time basis as we could on a war-time basis. Do I answer my hon. friend?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Well, not quite.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then let him ask more questions. I am completely prepared to give a reason for the hope within me.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am particularly interested in the things that are in short supply, the things we have to import. How would our capacity to produce affect those goods we have to import, those goods that are in short supply?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
As far as I have been able to find out, there is no difficulty in getting the goods we need from outside, with very few exceptions. I will grant that bringing in goods from the United States is causing us a certain amount of embarrassment because we are finding it hard to get United States dollars. But if we look about in various parts of the world I think we shall find that we can obtain from elsewhere the goods we are now buying from the United States. I think we shall find it completely feasible to obtain the goods we need, but which we cannot produce in Canada, from countries that will be quite happy to accept our goods. I do not want to get out of order; I just want to use this as an illustration, and I draw the Chairman's attention to that fact. May I point out to the hon. member that, for example, under the sugar policy this country has been following for the last three or four years, the policy it is following today, there appears to be no anxiety whatever about getting goods from outside. We insist on bringing sugar from outside instead of producing it in Canada, where we could produce two or three times our total consumption if we began to use the resources at our disposal. I would say there is no doubt whatever that this nation can produce or trade for goods necessary to give every man, woman and child in the country a very high standard of living; and the fact that the $11-8 billion worth of goods we produced in 1944 would amout to $983 for each man, woman and child indicates quite clearly that what I have said is in moderation. The only problem we face is how to get the money and how to put the money into the hands of the people. We can produce the goods. The only difficulty with us is to distribute the goods.
I do not wish to go into this any farther at the moment, unless hon. members wash to ask other questions. However I will say to hon. gentlemen across the way who are interested in this matter that if they will bring up their questions when they will be completely in order, I will go to any degree

_____________Emergency Powers
of scientific exposition to show that what I am saying is correct, and I can call to my support the best economic knowledge obtainable in Canada. Perhaps no more need be said tonight.
I should like to go on and repeat once more that this old age pension question is a dominion problem. The Minister of Justice has said that it is a provincial problem. We will grant that under the British North America Act such matters as the old age pension come within the responsibility of the provinces, but it has been clearly proved that the majority of the provinces are unable to find the money, because they do not have the taxation fields; and in many cases the taxation fields they were given under the British North America Act have been invaded by the dominion. The result is that there is only one authority that has the taxing power to get the revenue with which to do the things which ought to be done by way of social services.
One more matter must be borne in mind. What I have said indicates quite clearly that I believe that the money must ultimately be created by the federal government, as hon. members have heard me argue many times. Only one authority in Canada has that power to create money, and that is the dominion government. That is so because the British North America Act gave the dominion government control over banking, currency and coinage. From every angle and from every consideration it must be obvious that the dominion government must assume responsibility for old age pensions.
I say once more, in closing, that we should not even consider old age pensions of less than $50 a month at the age of sixty-five, without a means test, and with free medical, hospital and dental care.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope we do not make this a political issue. It would be a great pity, because I believe if I had before me the election literature of all parties-and I have not-I could show that every party promised better old age pensions. I do not think it is a political issue at all; and I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not so sensitive about what he is to bring before the house next Monday that he found it necessary to go out of his way to pick a quarrel with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I
I believe the country must recognize the fact that, as the span of life is extending, people are going to live longer, and as our civilization proceeds and our industrial organi-

zation develops, people are not going to be able in the future to work as many years in industry.
The other day I had a letter from an old person in Vancouver who made the statement that a number of firms in that city had already given notice that, after a certain date, all persons of sixty-five years of age would be out of employment. The gap between the ages of sixty-five and seventy has already appeared. Where will people of sixty-five go to look for work, with all the veterans back, and when women are being dismissed because the veterans are back?
Every day letters come to my desk from able-bodied women who do not know which way to turn because they are being let out of government services and other kinds of employment. If those able-bodied young people cannot find work, where is the person of sixty-five years of age to go for his livelihood in the time before the old age pension becomes effective? In the face of rising living costs, I do not know what these old people are going to do.
A pensioner said to me today-and this was not an old age pensioner, but one in a different category-"It will not make any difference to me if butter goes off the ration, because at sixty cents a pound I am not going to be able to buy butter." Dry bread for old age pensioners will not be a very happy thing in this country. Appetites of old age pensioners are not good at any time; they require special diets. I submit that, with butter at sixty cents a pound and a pension of $30 a month, old age pensioners will be eating dry bread, and they are not going to be able to have much milk, meat or those other things which enter into an adequate diet.
We ought not to let this become a partisan issue. It is a problem which has to do with a very large section of our population, and one in which you and I are involved personally-because we are the people who raised our own salaries last year, and made $2,000 of it income tax free. I, for one, did not support this, and I served notice on my caucus that I would not vote for it. I think that last year we should have made provision for the old age pensioners before we made provision for ourselves. Last year, time and again the government stalled off dealing with this problem, saying that the time was not yet.
If this matter is to be brought up next Monday, with respect to the increasing of pensions, I trust that the government will see fit to do more than add $5 to the pension which is now so inadequate, in the face of rising living costs. Rents are up; milk is up;

Emergency Powers
butter is up; bread is going up; sugar is going up. How can these people live? How can their families afford to help them, when the sons and daughters of these people are going to have the greatest difficulty in meeting their food budget and their own family needs?
The government was to be commended last year when it decided to pay family allowances in cash to all parents in this country. That was a sensible and businesslike way of attacking the problem of family allowances.
I say it should now do the same thing in respect of old age pensions. All persons over sixty-five years should be paid a superannuation allowance, and the income tax mechanism should be used to recover excess income, beginning on the same level with other persons who pay income tax. I do not know why we should segregate and treat as social lepers the people who did the pioneering in this country, and laid the foundation of our prosperity of today.
I was sorry the hon. member for Rosthern tried to confuse the issue in my province. We realize we are one of the poorest provinces in Canada; but in spite of our lack of provincial income we have done much more than the previous government did, and more than our resources warranted.
Again I say this should not become a political issue. And in order that everyone in Canada at the age of seventy may receive the same treatment, it should be paid on a federal *basis, and not be left to the discretion of the provinces to decide how they shall treat their pensioners. We did not do that in respect of family allowances. We said that all children in Canada have an equal claim to security. I think that likewise the pioneers in Canada have an equal claim to social security.
This should be universal superannuation, and they should begin to pay income tax on the same level as other people. In that way we would begin to put a floor under the family income of even old age pensioners.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss briefly another angle in connection with old1 age pensions which has always interested me. I agree with what has been said by the hon. mmebers for Winnipeg North Centre, Lethbridge and Qu'Appelle. There is another angle I would place before the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Finance and the government generally. It has to do with our whole system of living. I am assuming that we are earnest and sincere-and I believe we are-when we say we believe in the family unit. But the family unit presupposes that one member of
the family will be the breadwinner; and, generally speaking, we look upon the man as being in that position. If he does not supply the necessities for his family, but is in a position to do so, we take the necessary court action to see that some of his earnings are diverted to that purpose.
There is another angle which enters into this matter. I do not know the percentage, but I should imagine: it is a high percentage of the marriages which take place in Canada in which the man is several years older than the woman. If he is twenty-five and she is twenty-two we say to him, "Henceforth, and for the balance of your lives, you will be the breadwinner for the family, so long as you are able, and are earning. You must provide for your wife and family." Then, also, when a person reaches seventy years of age we say that we will pay an old age pension. So when the breadwinner becomes seventy years of age he-because in the majority of cases it is the husband-is entitled to the old age pension. He has a wife who is dependent upon him but he is told, "You must provide for this woman; while we recognize your needs and are going to pay you an old age pension, you will have to find some other means of carrying out your family responsibility and looking after your wife. Heretofore your earnings were supposed to do that but now your earnings have ceased. You are to receive from the nation for your pioneer work $30 a month-or whatever the amount will be; it varies in the different provinces-and either your wife will have to live on that with you, thereby reducing the standard of living for both of you, or she will have to go out and get a job." The wife is probably ill-equipped to do that. She will have spent all her life raising a family and will not be able to get a job except perhaps as a charwoman, and she would be too old to do that. The wife in many cases has not reached the age where she would be eligible for a pension.
It seems to me that that is manifestly unfair and uneconomical. It does not gibe with our belief in the family institutions of this country. When I have spoken of this I have heard it argued that if this is done there will be young women marrying these old age pensioners. I do not believe that is a sound argument, because most of the young women in this country are too sensible to do that. There may be the odd case and that may happen now and again, but it is not a major factor. I believe this government would be well advised to take this into consideration.
It is only fair that the wife and mother, who usually is younger than the husband, who
Emergency Powers

has spent her lifetime in. assisting her husband in his work and in the responsibilities of raising a family, should be recognized as being entitled to a pension.

I am going to suggest to the minister that before he brings down his old age pensions bill, before he sets an amount in that bill, he consider having the bill referred to a committee, probably after second reading. Then that committee should set up a budget for an old age pensioner, not to allow anything lavish, but just from a practical point of view. It has been suggested that perhaps some of the members of the committee might try to live on that budget for a month to see how it goes. I think in that way we could get some reasonable amount, and I am sure the Minister of Health and Welfare will see that no $30 a month can meet the requirements.
I join with the hon. member for Swift Current in what he said with regard to pensions paid to elderly people, especially when the man of the family is the only one receiving a pension. I have had instances of that kind brought to my attention, instances where two people had to live on the $25 or $30 a month which the husband was receiving. When we speak of $30 or $35 as being given in some of the provinces we must remember that that is not the amount of the old age pension being paid all across Canada. In fact, the pensions being paid in some of the other provinces are a great deal less than $30 or $35 a month.
We should look at this matter from a humane point of view, and not adopt the attitude taken by the Minister of Justice a while ago when he said, "Well, what about taxes?" There is one important aspect of this matter that I wish to develop before the order passes. In view of the fact
that the cost of living is increasing rapidly and that the old age pensioners are in no position to protect themselves against such increase, I would suggest that the minister give serious consideration to including in these orders for their duration, if the bill is not to come into effect in the near future, the idea of a cost of living supplement in connection with old age pensions. I would remind the committee that Canada cannot afford to be niggardly with our elderly citizens. During the years of the war a very large number of jmung, able-bodied men and women from our farms, factories and mines served with distinction in the army, the air force and the navy, and those of us who remained at home were able to establish new records in the field of production on our farms, in the forests, in the mines and factories of the country. We were able to give away enormous quantities of our Canadian products. Now that the war is over, now that we have all our people available to produce goods and to perform services on the Canadian scene, I cannot think of any good reason why our people should find, in the year 1947, that they have to consume less food and wear shoddier clothing,^ and find it more difficult to visit the dentist-why in general they should have to put up with a lower standard of living.
I think the government deserves a great deal of credit for formulating, during the war, fiscal policies that distributed, on a more equitable basis than ever before, available supplies of butter, sugar and other commodities in short supply. We were able to supply the people with larger quantities of most commodities than they ever enjoyed before. I cannot see any reason why we cannot look forward to increasing our local consumption, and particularly by the people in the old age pension brackets.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare made some remarks regarding the treatment given old age pensioners in Saskatchewan as compared with other provinces. I would point out to him that he lives in a province where, throughout many years, the people have been able to organize the Canadian economy so that they can keep a lion's share of our national income here. Again I quote from one of the government publications. In Ontario you have only one per cent of the married men receiving incomes of less than $250 in 1942, whereas in the prairie provinces you have three per cent of the married people who reported that income in the same period. You cannot blame the C.C.F. government for the very low incomes that prevail, but the fact is that in the prairie provinces three per cent of the male wage-earners had an annua! in-

Emergency Powers
come of less than $250, when these statistics were compiled. For the group receiving less than $1,000 you have only fourteen per cent in Ontario as compared with twenty-one per cent in the prairie provinces.
Obviously, where the income is on a much higher level in the wealthy province of Ontario, it should be possible for the people out of their consolidated revenue to provide more generous pensions and better social services than we can in a poor province like Saskatchewan. But I will not admit that the old age pensioners of Ontario are better off than those of Saskatchewan. The minister carefully refrained from specifying that conditions were better for them in Ontario than in Saskatchewan. Taking into account cash payable to the pensioner, hospital, medical, dental and optical services provided everyone receiving an old age pension, I think the pensioners in Saskatchewan are a good deal better off.
I hope the minister will take into considera-ation the rising cost of living and the need for seeing that, as the cost of living goes up, the old age pensioners shall not be required to do without butter. I find that on January 1, 1945, the cost of food, taking 1935-39 as basic 100, stood at 130-2. In January, 1946, it was 132-8 and in January, 1947, it was 145-5.
The old age pensioners are not like businessmen, who can anticipate what will happen to the market. They are at the mercy of the federal government, which controls the quality and quantity of what they eat.

We should approach this problem in a practical and realistic way. We should examine the weaknesses of the present act. I have listened to the discussion this evening and. in the main, I have noticed that the tendency is to treat our old people as paupers. Of course that is a weakness of the present legislation. Old people have to be reduced to a state of pauperism before they are eligible for old age pensions. Therefore my first thought would be to remove that cause. In other words, the method that we are employing is putting a premium upon thrift, and a thrifty nation is a worthy nation financially and physically, if I may use that term. I would suggest that in any approach to dealing with this problem we should remove the means test, so that these old people will be privileged to set something by for themselves in the days that are to come.
As the hon. member for Calgary West said, while we are all prone and glad to pay tribute to the pioneers who laid the foundation of this great country, yet we must constantly remember that others made a contribution who are not recipients of old age pensions at the present time. I would seek to remove the present stigma which goes with pensions. I do not know whether that is done or not, but I would remove all reference to old age pension and I would call it a retirement allowance. I would seek to emphasize the word "retirement", indicating, as it were, that when one reached the age of seventy he had reached the retirement age and that this was a retirement allowance. It must be remembered that when one receives a retirement allowance or an old age pension, even under the present regulations, no one can avoid admitting that one who has lived a lifetime must have made some contribution to the welfare o fthis country. It could be

Emergency Powers
considered a reward for services. On the other hand, if I were to compare the man who made himself a million with the other, it must be admitted that the former has taken more from the country in comparison with the '6'ther who has made his contribution throughout his life.
Those are the thoughts I have in mind. When the resolution is introduced I hope that the minister will take into consideration the one great weakness, as I see it, which does put a premium on thrift, and will still leave to the individual the hope that he can provide for himself, remove the means test and give the old age pension to everyone, and call it a retirement allowance.	.

Having listened all night, I think that I should say just a word or two before the order is passed, but not with the intention of trying to cover everything that has been said. As I have already interjected, a bill will be brought in when there will be a full opportunity to discuss the measures which have thus far been discussed.
However there are one or two things I wish to say at this stage, in view of what has already been said. As the hon. member for Calgary West has just pointed out, no one in this committee has any monopoly on interest, not only in the aged but in all the people of this country. No matter in what part of the house we sit, let it be assumed that no one has a monopoly on interest in this important problem. I want to say this for one thing, and one does not like to say it, but sitting here as the minister responsible for this particular measure, I take second place to no one in this committee-not that I have any prior right over anyone-because of my own background, a background which is similar to that of so many members of this committee. None of us have had silver spoons in our mouths from the beginning. The vast majority of members of this committee came from poor beginnings. That is why I say that every man in this chamber is aware of the problem. When one is in government, one must consider the problem in all of its contexts. One has to consider the matter in terms of other measures of social security and not only in terms of a particular measure such as the one we are now considering. To the hon. gentleman who has just spoken I say that the government has given this matter a great deal of thought. I do not suspect for one moment that the measure to be brought in will meet the point of view of everyone, but in the

light of all our responsibilities toward the aged, toward the young and toward other groups, it does represent what, under all the circumstances, seems most practicable for us to do at this time. The government that is proposing to bring in legislation is a government which has not been without great interest in social reform. It was this party which brought in old age pensions in the first instance. I am sure that will not be forgotten.

I wish to say a few words before this carries. Because of the importance of the matter now under discussion for the welfare of our old citizens, I consider it my duty to put our stand on the record right now. Of course I do not intend to speak at length on the problem, especially because a resolution is announced for Monday. Nevertheless I want to say tonight that we favour a substantial increase in the old age pension, one which will cover the increase in the cost of living and will also assure an improvement in the condition of the old age pensioners. So far as the means test is -concerned, we think it should, in principle, be abolished.
The last point I wish to make clear tonight is that the age of the pensioners should be reduced. For the future, as soon as unemployment seems to face our country, this age should be considerably reduced. But in the present situation, because of the tremendous needs of manpower, especially in housing activities, I think it would be fair to fix the age at sixty-five for a year or two, particularly for those who at this age are still able and willing to enter the regular labour market.
